articles.title: Pension Is Wall Street's Casino
articles.author: Ellen Brown/Web of Debt
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. “Most billionaires don’t park their money in making more businesses. They park their money in the stock market. That is not meaningfully investing in opportunity, it’s just investing in other billionaires.” So said Abdul El-Sayed , U.S. Senator-elect from Michigan. He said that he would rather “have an economy that makes a thousand millionaires than one billionaire,” and that money that would otherwise go into the S&P 500 should go instead to “good schools, good infrastructure, health care, child care.” It’s a laudable sentiment, but those thousand millionaires would probably still be parking their money in investments designed to make more money without producing anything. When an investor buys Nvidia shares on the stock market, the money goes to whoever sold the shares, not to Nvidia. A company gets new capital only when it issues new stock. The profits from stock market trades go either to the buyer or the seller, depending on which way the penny falls. And it’s not just the billionaires and millionaires playing those financial markets. Our household savings, corporate funds and pension funds are gambling there as well. State and local pension funds hold $6.2 trillion , more than a fifth of the GDP of the U.S. economy. That massive pool of money is not building housing, infrastructure or local businesses. It is parked in Wall Street’s casino, bidding up the price of existing assets, while asset managers collect their fees whether the pension funds win or lose. And many pundits are predicting an imminent market crash, in which the funds will lose big. Worse, the returns to the pension funds are no better than they could get from a simple index fund without incurring outside management fees, and sometimes they are worse. Meanwhile, the nation’s only state-owned bank, the Bank of North Dakota, earned a 17.2% return on its capital in 2025 while lending into its state’s own economy, and paid $258 million of its profits back to the state. North Dakota’s money is safe, earning, and invested in local productivity. Related: AI Abundance: Meaning Beyond Work The House Always Wins “Everything feels like a casino,” said UK financial commentator Anna Bocca in a March 2026 video titled “ How Financialisation Rewired the Economy .” “ Financialization ” is the process by which financial markets and institutions have gained growing influence over economic policy and investing, shifting the focus from making physical goods and services to using money to make more money. The “house” in today’s financial casino is the asset manager collecting our pension money – Bocca names BlackRock, State Street, and Vanguard – and the house wins even when the pensioners lose. Consider New York City. Its five pension funds held $326.3 billion as of June 30, 2026. The city pays about $10 billion a year into them, even as it struggles to close a projected $5.4 billion budget deficit. What does the city get for its money? In 2015, then-Comptroller Scott Stringer examined ten years of results from the asset managers running the city’s pension funds. Managers of public stocks and bonds had beaten their benchmarks (the returns the same money would have earned in a standard market index such as the S&P 500) by $2.063 billion. But that was before deducting the managers’ fees. The fees consumed more than 95% of the gain, leaving the funds only an estimated $40 million ahead. Managers of the funds’ private investments (stakes in assets not traded on public exchanges, such as private equity and real estate funds) fell $2.6 billion short of their benchmarks after fees. Overall, the outside managers fell more than $2.5 billion dollars short of benchmark returns over the ten year period. The pension funds would have done better in plain index funds. “Right now, heads or tails, Wall Street wins,” Stringer said . Stringer’s study was cited by Scott Baker, managing editor at OpEdNews and a Public Banking Institute expert on pension funds, in a November 2025 article titled “ The Case for Selling off the New York City Pension Funds .” Baker asks, “Why do we need pension funds at all?” More on his answer after a look at pension fund financing as it has evolved over the last half-century. Related: The Digital Dollar That Was Too Democratic to Survive How Our Pensions Got into the Casino The evolution of pension fund financing was traced in a July 2025 report from the American Federation of Teachers (AFT) and other sponsors titled “ From Public Pensions to Private Fortunes: How Working People’s Retirements Line Billionaire Pockets .” The authors observed that before 1980, state and local pension funds were often treated as a “pay as you go” system: a portion of current employee premiums was used to pay benefits to retirees, similar to Social Security. Then a new “actuarial” accounting approach began treating any shortfall between a fund’s assets and its future obligations as an “unfunded” liability. The pressure to close that apparent gap “drove an unprecedented accumulation of assets” – money-producing investments such as stocks, bonds, real estate and stakes in private equity. Between 1980 and 2007, state and local pension assets grew from $183 billion to $3.2 trillion, from 6% to 23% of GDP. By 2024, they stood at $6.2 trillion (an equivalent percentage of GDP, which had also grown). Tom Sgouros, a public finance consultant, former senior policy advisor to the Rhode Island General Treasurer and fellow at Brown University’s Policy Lab, has questioned the need for this accumulation of financial assets at the expense of productive investment. In a 2022 report for the National Conference on Public Employee Retirement Systems , he pointed out that a public pension plan, unlike a private one, “need not worry about the disappearance of its sponsoring employer,” in this case the city. Cities can go bankrupt, but they will always be there. A new government will just replace the old one. Until the 1960s, according to a November 2024 housing report co-authored by Sgouros for Americans for Financial Reform (AFR) and Georgetown University, it was “unremarkable” for pension funds to invest in state and local government bonds. Today, however, it is rare. Most municipal bonds are tax-exempt and pay lower interest rates than corporate bonds; and pension funds, which pay no taxes, get no benefit from the tax break. The older arrangement, which Sgouros calls “fiscal mutualism,” meant that public workers’ savings financed public needs: their pension funds lent to their own cities and states for schools and other projects, and were paid back with interest. This mutually beneficial arrangement unraveled when pension funds began chasing higher yields in corporate bonds, forcing local governments to borrow on the open market at higher rates and fees. Meanwhile, most private sector workers have lost their guaranteed pensions altogether. According to a March 2026 Congressional Research Service report , only 14% of private sector workers had access in 2025 to a “defined benefit” pension (one that guarantees a set monthly payment for life, usually based on salary and years of service), compared to 70% with access to a “defined contribution” plan such as a 401(k), whose value rises and falls with the markets. Related: AI Abundance and the Future of Freedom “Patsies for the Private Equity Industry” According to Reason Foundation data , in 2001 public pension funds held 57.7% of their assets in publicly-traded stocks, 31.4% in bonds, and 9% in “alternatives” — private equity, hedge funds, real estate and commodities. By fiscal year 2024, 34% of pension fund investments were in the alternatives, which carry significantly more costs and risks even than the stock market. Private equity (PE) is particularly risky and controversial. It relies heavily on borrowed money, and investors must commit their money for ten years or more. The management fees are also far higher – typically 2% of asset values plus 20% of profits – and according to the AFT report, “PE managers frequently manipulate reported asset values.” Correcting for these factors, the report concludes, private equity’s “yield advantage is little more than a mirage, facilitated by leverage used for buyouts.” Yet public pension funds are the biggest backers of the private equity industry. According to the AFT report, public pensions “make up almost a third of all investors to private equity funds and contribute an astonishing 67 percent of their capital.” PE firms are notorious for the leveraged buyout, described by the AFR housing report as “using a company’s own assets to finance its takeover by private investors and then looting them after: selling off real estate, closing pension plans, abruptly shuttering less-profitable divisions and major layoffs.” Employment at companies bought by private equity shrinks significantly, and a leveraged buyout can result in bankruptcy. The report points to the devastating collapse of two private equity-owned hospital chains, Steward Health Care and Prospect Medical Holdings. What do the pension funds get for backing PE firms? In a 2020 study titled “ An Inconvenient Fact: Private Equity Returns & The Billionaire Factory ,” Oxford professor Ludovic Phalippou found that private equity funds “have returned about the same as public equity indices since at least 2006.” Yet the performance fees on funds raised from 2006 to 2015 were estimated at $230 billion. In an interview, Phalippou called it a “wealth transfer from several hundred million pension scheme members to a few thousand people working in private equity,” one that “might be one of the largest in the history of modern finance.” In an April 2024 podcast , financial journalist Bethany McLean countered the fiction that pension fund managers are sophisticated investors, stating, “ They’re just the patsies for the private equity industry .” Related: Fed Regime Change: From Big Bank Bailouts to Local Productivity Bailing Out the Casino Privatization, says Bocca, has “shifted all financial risk and reward away from the state and onto the individual pensioner,” while funneling trillions of dollars into the hands of global asset managers. BlackRock alone now manages a record $15.3 trillion . Bocca describes the pursuit of shareholder profit over company productivity as “cost cutting instead of long-term innovation, debt loading instead of reinvestment, outsourcing instead of stable employment, stock buybacks instead of wage growth.” When a private equity firm loads a company with debt and it collapses, “it’s often the workers, residents, or taxpayers who end up bearing the consequences.” Asset managers’ fees grow with the size of the pool, not necessarily with its performance; and when markets crash, the losses are absorbed by the pensioners. A case in point is Blackstone, considered the world’s largest asset manager and the largest landlord in the United States. Blackstone is funded by CalPERS and many other public pension funds. In 2021, it bought 5,600 affordable housing units in San Diego and raised rents by 43% to 65% in two years. “Among the most troubling aspects of the housing crisis,” wrote the authors of the AFR housing report, “is the extent to which workers’ own capital is being used to make it worse.” The pension fund that is supposed to secure a teacher’s retirement may be financing the landlord raising her rent. The asset managers’ fastest growing product is private credit — loans made directly to companies by investment funds rather than banks. According to the AFT report, private credit loans “are not regulated and not covered by securities laws or even rated,” and private credit “also relies heavily on public pensions.” It is now seeing rising defaults on its loans, which are often to companies owned by PE firms. Yet an August 2025 executive order directed regulators to ease the way for private equity and other alternative assets to be included in 401(k) plans. When the whole casino is in trouble, the public again bails it out. When markets froze in March 2020, the Federal Reserve hired BlackRock to manage its new corporate debt-buying programs. The flood of central bank money lifted asset prices, and those who owned the most assets gained the most. According to Oxfam, billionaires’ wealth rose more in the first 24 months of Covid-19 than in the previous 23 years combined. “Investors keep the upside,” says Bocca. “Society absorbs the downside.” Today, Moneywise reports , the U.S. has a record 989 billionaires, and the 400 wealthiest Americans are worth a record $8 trillion , up from $6.6 trillion a year earlier. Related: Rethinking America’s Financial Plumbing: The Wealth Concentration Engine A Better Way: Pay As You Go, and a Public Bank Scott Baker’s proposal for New York City is to get out of the money-making-money business altogether. The city could guarantee retirees their current benefits plus annual cost-of-living increases, and pay them as Social Security does, from current revenues. It could lay off the outside investment managers and sell off the fund assets gradually over about five years. Part of the proceeds could pay down city debt, immediately raising the city’s credit rating and lowering borrowing costs. The rest could capitalize a public bank. Baker envisions a bank with about $50 billion in deposits, lending to local small businesses and individuals that large commercial banks pass over. The stellar U.S. model is the Bank of North Dakota (BND), founded in 1919. By law , state funds are deposited in the BND, which uses them to back loans into the state, mostly in partnership with local banks. As noted above, BND earned net income of $231.8 million in 2025 – a 17.2% return – and paid $210 million into the state’s general fund and another $48.3 million to other state funds. There is no house taking a cut. Momentum for public banks is building around the country, as detailed at a Public Banking Institute conference in Philadelphia on October 22-24. In Washington State and New Mexico , enthusiastic support for public bank bills followed presentations earlier this year by BND president Don Morgan on the mechanics and benefits of the BND. City-owned banks are also in the works. On October 21, the Los Angeles City Council voted 11 to 3 to identify $460,000 for a feasibility study for a city-owned bank; and on November 3, two other California cities voted on public bank initiatives. San Francisco’s Proposition B would create a municipal finance corporation as the first step toward a city-owned public bank, and Berkeley voters will decide on a citizen-initiated parcel tax that would raise $58 million over six years to capitalize a public bank. Neither vote had been called as of November 5; California can take up to 30 days to finalize votes. In Philadelphia, where the City Council voted in 2022 to create a Public Financial Authority as a first step toward a public bank, advocates are pushing “ Project Beloved Community ,” a ten-year plan that includes a city public bank and proposes investing city pension funds in local housing, clean energy and community-owned businesses. In New York City, Mayor Mamdani and Comptroller Levine have begun moving city deposits to community lenders , a first step while advocates press Albany to pass the New York Public Banking Act . And at the national level, The National Infrastructure Bank Act , HR 5356, now has 65 co-sponsors. The money is already ours — our pension contributions, our tax dollars and our public deposits. Rather than handing it to a casino where the house always wins and the pensioners absorb the losses, we can put it to work building homes, businesses and infrastructure in our own communities, and keep the profits for ourselves. Web of Debt This article was first posted as an original to ScheerPost.com .

articles.title: Remembering Dolores Huerta (1930-2026)
articles.author: DSA Religion and Socialism Working Group
articles.content: Dolores Huerta , who died on October 28 at the age of 96, was an honorary chair of DSA from 2012-2016. But her involvement with our organization went back as far as being a speaker at a 1975 convention of one of DSA’s predecessor organizations. My wife, Dolores Delgado-Campbell, and I met her even earlier,when we were co-chairs of the United Farm Workers (UFW) lettuce boycott committee in Sacramento. We entered the fray in 1972 when the corrupt leadership of the Teamsters Union signed sweetheart contracts with grape growers, committing one of the worst examples of union betrayal in U.S. history. These contracts effectively ended the grape strike of mostly Mexican American and Filipino workers that many churches and synagogues had supported. Working with Dolores and the UFW for the next decade shaped our own political and career paths and broadened our political perspectives. We paid a political cost, too. In 1973, because of her involvement in the lettuce boycott, Dolores Campbell was not rehired (i.e., de facto fired) from her position teaching Women ’s History and Mexican American History at American River College in Sacramento. After a seven-year struggle and assistance from her union, she regained the position and became a sought after professor. In a satisfying footnote to history, more than 50 years after her association with Huerta and la causa made her persona non grata, she brought Huerta to a celebration of women’s history at the college in 2012. The auditorium was filled with students, faculty and staff trying to get into the room. Dolores Huerta was a relentless bundle of spirit and energy, and it was almost impossible to say “No” to her, in large part because she always worked longer and harder than anyone else. Dolores was also a persistent supporter of DSA’s own Latino Commission (1983- 2004). She is best known for her co-founding of the United Farm Workers union with Cesar Chavez and many others including former DSA honorary chair Eliseo Medina, Philip Vera Cruz, and Larry Itleong. Her influence has been profound. The creation of the UFW changed the nature of labor organizing in the Southwest and contributed significantly to the growth of Latino politics in the United States.Her frequent public engagements at colleges, universities, and high schools, where she brought a Latina feminist perspective to labor, civil rights , and immigration issues highlights her long history and personal commitment to movement building. That commitment to community mobilization against corporate power produced a backlash against her. Texas even banned textbooks on U.S. history because they included her story. On the other hand, when I contributed to a popular history book for middle-school students, The Americans: A History of the United States (1970 & 1979), we included a recording Dolores made in 1968. After leaving UFW leadership in 1994, Dolores traveled the country organizing and encouraging women to step up and take leadership roles in unions , politics, and more. She grew to become one of the leading feminist leaders in the nation focusing particularly on empowering young women and Latinas. Dolores was raised in the Catholic faith, and her lifetime of work demonstrated her commitment to the ideals of the struggle for social justice.Her thinking evolved constantly. Earlier in her life, she was against abortion ; later she was a champion of reproductive justice. Her intensive work, recognized when President Barack Obama presented her with the Presidential Medal of Freedom, illustrated how the fight for union rights and wages also included the fight for women’s leadership in unions, immigrant justice , and reproductive freedom. In the last year of her life she broke a decades-long silence about being assaulted as a young woman by Cesar Chavez and spoke of the misogyny within the farmworker movement, the labor movement, and society in general. We consider ourselves blessed to have had many opportunities to learn from Dolores and to have worked alongside her in campaigns. For more information about her lifetime of union and social justice work, read her story at In Memory of Dolores Huerta . Author Duane Campbell, Dolores Delgado-Campbell, and Dolores Huerta in 2014 . The post Remembering Dolores Huerta (1930-2026) appeared first on DSA Religious Socialism .

articles.title: Israel’s Shaky Democracy Continues to Crumble
articles.author: Jared Hillel
articles.content: In July 1950, speaking at the annual Zionist Organization of America convention, US Vice President Alben W. Barkley asserted that Israel was “an oasis of liberty in the desert of despotism,” articulating a precursor to the oft-repeated adage “Israel is the only democracy in the Middle East.” While the expression cannot be traced to a singular person, the sentiment that Israel — a nation with free elections and civil liberties — stands alone amid a sea of authoritarian regimes has been cultivated by Western institutions and Israeli leaders since the state was founded. From the outset, Israel’s earliest laws legalizing persecution against Palestinians showed the incompatibility between Jewish supremacy and democracy. But the subjugation of one group is rarely self-contained, and throughout history, illiberal nations have almost always turned against a portion of their citizens, often as violence against the outgroup reaches its peak. In the midst of the bloodiest three years in the country’s history, and particularly during the election campaign, this tendency began to play out. Israel has disenfranchised voters , at times even contradicting its own discriminatory laws, in efforts to marginalize Jews perceived as a threat to Benjamin Netanyahu and his increasingly violent political agenda. Barriers to the Ballot In the past three years, emigration from Israel has reached record heights. According to a study published by Tel Aviv University, 270,000 citizens have left the country in the past three years. Between 2013 and 2015, the corresponding period in the previous decade, the number sat at 183,000. Like much of the American Jewish diaspora , those who have left in recent years have become deeply critical of Benjamin Netanyahu. While Israel guarantees every citizen over the age of eighteen the right to vote, it has never permitted absentee ballots. With the exception of diplomats , emissaries, and Israel Defense Forces (IDF) soldiers occupying territory in Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria, voters must be in the country on Election Day. With this election largely seen as one of the most consequential in the nation’s history, a survey taken before the election estimated that up to 67,000 expats could be returning home to vote. On October 27, Likud won twenty-seven seats, and Gad Eisenkot’s Yashar party won twenty-one. Netanyahu’s bloc took fifty-three seats, against forty-eight for the Jewish opposition bloc and nineteen for the Arab-led parties. No bloc won the sixty-one seats needed for a majority. The results have left the country facing uncertain coalition negotiations. Leading up to the vote, Likud tried to stop Israelis outside the country from coming back. In September, Likud petitioned the Central Election Committee, demanding it block Fly & Vote, an initiative by the nonpartisan American-Israel Democracy (AID) Coalition, which sought to help Israelis abroad return and cast a vote. Offering logistical help, including eligibility checks and passport renewals, the organization also coordinated six group flights and helped search for commercial flights. While participants were still required to pay their airfare, Likud argued the initiative violated financing laws and constituted election bribery. While the petition was ultimately dismissed, the AID Coalition agreed to not subsidize tickets, organize any additional group flights, or provide transportation and accommodation. This summer, a second spat broke out when hundreds of Israelis living abroad discovered they had been stripped of their voting rights after being classified by the Interior Ministry as nonresidents. The designation, known as Code 51, excluded citizens from the voter registry altogether. Petitioning the Supreme Court, the expats argued that they were not notified of their status change, with several only realizing when checking their electoral eligibility. The courts dismissed the case on procedural grounds, stating the claim was filed too late. While there is no definitive proof linking Likud to the Code 51 scandal, it is clear that the party has repeatedly tried to curtail the expat vote. Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported that informal discussions were held between senior Transport Ministry officials about the possibility of restricting designated landing slots at airports, making it more difficult to fly into the country. Similar to the proposed judicial reforms of 2023, where Netanyahu sought to weaken the power of the Supreme Court, this democratic backsliding has prompted furor among the Israeli left. But as is often the case with liberal Zionists, the far greater repression affecting Palestinians remains largely ignored. Defending the Ethnocracy The AID Coalition describes itself as a group “strengthening, and preserving the democratic foundations of the State of Israel.” While a valiant objective, a more honest statement would be about preserving an ethnocracy. Israeli Professor Oren Yiftachel describes this form of governance as one that “promotes the expansion of the dominant group in contested territory and its domination of power structures while maintaining a democratic facade.” This dynamic has been present since the state’s founding. While the 150,000 Palestinians who remained in their homeland after the Nakba were declared citizens and granted the right to vote from the beginning, the community also faced systematic discrimination from the outset. From 1948 until 1966, Palestinian citizens of Israel were placed under military rule , which included measures that restricted their movement, prohibited political organizing, and imposed arbitrary curfews. Simultaneously, the government confiscated hundreds of thousands of dunams of land, uprooting farmers from their livelihood and forcing many to turn to low-wage labor to survive. In 1967, a year after lifting the military administration, Israel would turn their attention toward Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza after occupying both territories in the Six-Day War. Assuming control of around one million Palestinians, residents of the newly occupied territory were placed under military rule. This time citizenship and the right to vote were withheld from them, since such incorporation would threaten the Jewish demographic majority. As Jewish settlers moved into the occupied territories, aided by generous Israeli government subsidies, an apartheid regime took shape, as authorities applied separate laws, courts, and democratic rights to Palestinians and Israelis living in neighboring areas. Although Israel disengaged from Gaza in 2005, it lay siege to the Strip two years later, imposing a crushing blockade. After the October 7 attacks, it returned yet again as the occupying power, this time unleashing a genocide that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians. In the West Bank, the apartheid regime continues, as roughly 500,000 settlers, excluding those in East Jerusalem, live with full rights outside of Israel’s internationally recognized border, beside Palestinians who cannot vote, travel freely, or even build on their ancestral land. Amid the dire situation in the West Bank and Gaza, the plight of Palestinians living inside Israel is largely forgotten. Yet these 2.1 million residents continue to live as second-class citizens. In 2018, the Israeli Knesset passed the quasi-constitutional Nation-State Law , stipulating that self-determination is unique to the Jewish people, without guaranteeing equality for its other citizens. Furthermore, Palestinian citizens of Israel continue to face entrenched discrimination in urban planning, economic development, and educational opportunities. The Authoritarian Turn In 2024, the Varieties of Democracy Institute downgraded Israel from a liberal to an electoral democracy. The demotion followed Netanyahu and his coalition’s attempt to overhaul the judiciary, their accusations the Supreme Court was “left-leaning,” and deterioration in protections against torture. This classification did not take into account the active atrocities that Israel was perpetrating in Gaza and the West Bank at the time. Yet since this reclassification, Netanyahu has shed more of the democratic facade he has long sought to uphold. More than five hundred humanitarian workers have been killed since the war in Gaza began. In December 2025, Israel attempted to bar thirty-seven nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) from operating in the West Bank and Gaza. The Supreme Court froze the ban, allowing the organizations to continue operating pending a final ruling. More recently, numerous foreign journalists have been turned away at the border during the election campaign, with others facing arduous interrogations and detention before being allowed entry. Perhaps most revealing is the government’s willingness to break long-standing supremacist laws, which uphold Jews as a privileged class in Israel. Starting in 2025, several Jewish activists were detained and deported for engaging in protective presence, a form of nonviolent solidarity work in which civilians deter violent settlers from harassing Palestinian communities. Earlier this year, a Jewish American academic on a three-year residency visa was denied entry after being accused of being a “left-wing anarchist.” After the backlash prompted by the film NAZA , in which IDF soldiers admitted to knowingly killing innocent civilians in Gaza, Netanyahu announced plans to introduce a bill that would strip those who defame the IDF of their Israeli citizenship. Last month, it was reported that two Jews were denied citizenship for having previously partaken in anti-occupation activism in the West Bank. This was the first known case of the state violating the Law of Return, which stipulates that every Jew is entitled to immigrate to Israel. Many saw Gad Eisenkot as the last chance to halt the country’s authoritarian drift. The election has left open the possibility that he could still lead the government, but he has no clear path to power. While he might reverse the emerging trend of discriminating against Jews and Israelis deemed insufficiently patriotic, none of his proposed policies address the core issues that make Israel an ethnostate. The election has not changed the reality for Palestinians, with or without Israeli citizenship, or the refusal of every major party to address these injustices. What Eisenkot may offer is merely a return to the illusion of democracy. articles.title: Medi-Cal Crisis Deepens
articles.author: Mark Kreidler
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. I met Rena Salamacha last summer, when the worst of H.R. 1’s cuts to federal Medicaid funding weren’t yet finalized, only feared. Salamacha, CEO of Mee Memorial Healthcare System in Monterey County, knew then that the system’s medical center in King City, serving rural and mostly low income patients, was already in trouble. “We don’t have services to cut,” the CEO said simply. More than a year later, that remains the reality. After all the shouting over Prop. 40, and the massive investment of time and money by California’s billionaire class to defeat the tax , the state’s fragile health care ecosystem is in the same place it was last week: trying, as Salamacha tries every week , to find ways to keep going. That road is about to get rougher. The worst of the new federal Medi-Cal cuts and rules changes (including work requirements) will kick in beginning next year, and from the California vote totals available so far, there won’t be Prop. 40 money coming in to offset any of the reductions. The result: Increased strain on existing hospitals and clinics, fewer services available, and more people going uninsured. As always, this long-term structural problem will land on the state’s most vulnerable. California stands to lose an estimated $30 billion a year in federal funding for Medi-Cal, the low-income program upon which roughly 14 million residents – more than a third of our population, including 4.5 million kids – rely for their health care. Congratulations, Xavier Becerra: This is your problem now. Prop. 40 certainly wouldn’t solve the health care crisis in California, nor was it designed to. It was as it appeared: a one-time 5% wealth tax on the richest 250 people in the state, billionaires all, which would generate up to $100 billion in revenue over about five years. Almost all of the money was to be used to offset federal funding cuts to health care. Not every detail was ironed out, as was known. That included the question of how the state would go about valuing certain assets – art, wine, automobiles – that are part of many ultra-wealthy portfolios, as well as how the new tax revenue would be distributed among health care providers. Also known: The union that spearheaded the Prop. 40 drive represents health care workers whose jobs could be on the line if, as expected, California’s care system contracts in the absence of funding. Now state lawmakers and Becerra, the incoming governor, must search for ways to protect Medi-Cal for as many residents as possible, or else face a wave of uninsured patients who won’t stop needing care just because they can’t pay for services. As many as 1.3 million Californians could lose health insurance as a result of H.R. 1, according to estimates. Related: Trump's ICE Crackdown Sparks California Voter Suppression Fears First as a member of Congress and then as secretary of Health and Human Services under President Joe Biden, Becerra fought for decades to expand Medicaid at the federal level. More recently, he opposed Gov. Gavin Newsom’s move to scale back coverage for undocumented adult immigrants in California, a cause Newsom had championed but retreated from due to budget issues. California’s budget cannot backfill the steep H.R. 1 funding cuts, so it’s a matter of limiting the damage. Becerra, who says he wants the state to be “the backstop for health care,” has a few options. Institute a “fair share” tax. Becerra is a strong supporter of state legislation that would levy fines on businesses that have a large number of employees on Medi-Cal – in other words, tax those companies for paying their workers so little that they qualify for the low-income health care program. The state Department of Finance is studying what such a program would look like, with a presentation to state legislators expected next spring. Reduce waste. As a candidate, Becerra said that California is “losing billions to fraudulent claims and misused benefits.” He said that as governor, he’ll create a dedicated health care fraud task force to go after such activity. Becerra also pledged to modernize Medi-Cal’s’ system to include automatic state-generated renewals, which he said would reduce paperwork errors that lead to eligible patients being mistakenly dropped from coverage – an idea that will be sorely tested by H.R. 1 rules that now require twice-yearly requalifying. Related: California Saves Millions on Home Care: Workers Pay the Price Raise taxes on the wealthy. Becerra opposed the Prop. 40 wealth tax, but he has indicated he’s open to increasing taxes on top income earners. Becerra told KCRA in Sacramento that the idea is to go after that money “if we can prove that you’re not paying your fair share. And to me, that’s pretty basic: If you’re a billionaire and you’re paying at a lower tax rate than a firefighter, a teacher or a nurse, you’re not paying your fair share.” There are no details on such a plan, nor a timetable for implementation. Reallocate other state funding. This is the least likely of options, given the state’s estimated $18.5 billion operating deficit for 2026-27, but it is possible for the state to shift more funding toward Medi-Cal in an effort to hold the program together at its current levels of participation. From the time he began campaigning for governor in 2015, Newsom made health care a centerpiece of his platform. He specifically pointed toward creating a single-payer system, then backed off once in office, saying he hoped to achieve “universal access” to care instead. In the end, Newsom will leave the office with all of those notions incomplete. It’s a fair reflection of how, even in a willing and one-party controlled state, solving health care issues on a massive scale remains an elusive goal. Newsom also will hand off to Becerra a problem not of his making, with H.R. 1’s deepest cuts set to begin when the new governor takes office. Funding from Prop. 40 wouldn’t have erased that problem, but it might have bought Becerra and the legislature some time to consider options. Not any more. The clock is ticking. Capital & Main

articles.title: Austerity Is Now the Central Conflict in Brazilian Politics
articles.author: André Singer
articles.content: On October 4, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, finished the first round of Brazil’s presidential election nearly two points ahead of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Three weeks later, Lula turned the result around and won a fourth term in the October 25 runoff. In between, left-led demonstrations filled the streets of hundreds of Brazilian cities. The government also banned online betting, backed a forty-hour workweek, and raised the benefit of Bolsa Família, the cash-transfer program for poor families that Lula created in 2003. Few analysts know Lula’s political project better than André Singer. A professor of political science at the University of São Paulo, Singer served as Lula’s spokesperson from 2003 to 2007 and press secretary from 2005 to 2007. He developed the concept of Lulism in Os sentidos do lulismo (2012) and O lulismo em crise (2018), and his new book, Impasse: O Brasil diante da onda reacionária , came out in August. After the runoff, Singer spoke with Catarina Príncipe and Aldo Cordeiro Sauda for Jacobin about Bolsonarism as autocracy with a fascist bias, the Brazilian bourgeoisie’s silence during the campaign, and why the second-round mobilization was not populism. He also discussed the fight over austerity that awaits Lula’s fourth term. Catarina Príncipe You’ve written about the idea of an “autocracy with a fascist bias” to understand the phenomena of Donald Trump in the United States and Jair Bolsonaro in Brazil. Could you explain this idea further? André Singer Honestly, I can’t speak directly about Trumpism, because I don’t have enough expertise. So I’ll talk about Bolsonarism, the experience from which I formulated the idea of an autocratic tendency with a fascist bias. Studying the Bolsonaro presidency of 2019–2022, one can show empirically that he tried to reshape Brazil’s institutions in the direction of an autocratic regime. One of the major conflicts during his term was over the independence of the Federal Police. For an American audience: The Federal Police is equivalent to the FBI. It is a national police force for the country’s major security problems, because everyday problems fall to the state governments. But the big questions of corruption, organized crime, drug trafficking, and arms trafficking are all the Federal Police’s business. That is why a convention that successive presidents have observed since the return to democracy in the 1980s is so important: guaranteeing the Federal Police’s independence. The president of the republic appoints the director, but presidents have made a practice of appointing directors who have a certain independence from themselves. Bolsonaro made a point of violating that convention and appointing a Federal Police leadership at the service of his own political interests. I’m describing this because it is the most evident case of all: he tried to manipulate the Federal Police to concentrate power. Why do I say this autocratic tendency has a fascist bias? Because I find in it certain elements in common with historical fascism. Why don’t I say it’s fascist tout court? Because there are many elements that don’t correspond. Let me give one element in common: the activation, through propaganda, of the unconscious of the masses. It is a kind of advertising that aims to hook the voter, the citizen, and the supporter through unconscious identification rather than rational argument. That doesn’t mean there aren’t also arguments of a material nature, material interests; I’m not saying it is merely a technique aimed at the unconscious. But I think this is very typical of fascism and not of the nonfascist right. What isn’t in common with fascism? For example, there is no political party organized into militias, as in Italian fascism and then German Nazism. There is also no warlike rhetoric, in the sense of external war: Bolsonarism has a very strange nationalism of submission to the United States — something hard to understand. But it has no rhetoric of confrontation with other countries or of territorial expansion, an important element of historical fascism. Since some elements are in common and many are not, I proposed a way of understanding the Bolsonaro phenomenon. We are facing an autocratic tendency — that is proven — with a fascist tendency that we still need to test. Meanwhile, there is a more general theoretical problem: the concept of fascism isn’t well defined. Strange as it may seem, that is the problem we have to face: arriving at a concept of fascism that lets us understand the present situation. Obviously we are interested in understanding history, but with a view to the present and the future. Catarina Príncipe In an interview, I heard you distinguish between fascism from below and fascism from above. Which class does this autocracy with a fascist bias mobilize most? André Singer Marxist-inspired thought has already made clear the characteristics of historical fascism, and one stands out: fascism is a movement that comes from below, not from above. Leon Trotsky first made that contribution, in his writings on Germany, and it still holds; it is a fundamental distinction. Bolsonarism has this characteristic: it comes from below; it is not a movement of the ruling class. It draws in the middle strata, but it quickly spreads to intermediate popular layers, which form its backbone. So in Brazil today, the far right penetrates from below. Catarina Príncipe How do you analyze the relationship between the ruling class and politics, given the existence of what you call two cross-class coalitions: the Bolsonarist “confederacy” and the Lulist “ concertación ”? What is the composition of these two coalitions? André Singer I call one the “confederacy,” by a certain analogy with the nineteenth-century American case, and the other the “concertación,” by analogy with Chile after Augusto Pinochet. I developed these two hypotheses to understand the 2022 election. So I’ll answer with 2022 in mind, then briefly go through the changes in 2026. The idea of the confederacy was that a coalition of agribusiness entrepreneurs and service sector entrepreneurs in the cities formed. Certain evangelical denominations, which represent a kind of Brazilian Bible Belt, joined them. These denominations account for about 30 percent of the Brazilian electorate, and Bolsonarism has repeatedly won 70 percent of their vote. In the 2022 election, the whole of the security forces joined these two components, the entrepreneurs and the evangelical Bible Belt, from the armed forces down to the regional (state) police forces. These forces represent a large contingent. Besides everyone formally engaged in security work, Brazil has an enormous army of private security guards, because public security can’t cope with the very serious crime problem. These three tracks of the confederacy, so to speak, created an enormous corridor through the interior of the country. It runs from the north of Rio Grande do Sul to the south of the North Region, through the interior of São Paulo and Minas Gerais, the country’s most industrialized states. That corridor aligned with Bolsonarism, which largely explains its significant electoral power. In addition, the evangelical Bible Belt gives Bolsonarism a very strong bridgehead in Brazil’s large metropolitan regions. In 2026, there was a change: because of the failed coup attempt, the armed forces pulled back. They had been very important because Bolsonaro, a former army captain, went through the military academy with the men who, by coincidence, made up the high command when he took office. He brought them into the government, and so the armed forces were deeply committed to the Bolsonaro government. That is no longer the case. You can’t identify anyone of note from the armed forces in the campaign of his son Flávio Bolsonaro. But we know that the police forces backed that candidacy discreetly, rather than explicitly, as they had with Jair Bolsonaro’s government. I call it a confederacy, although it has no connection with slavery. But it does have this connection: it divided Brazil. It united the interior, as if against the big cities, even though, I repeat, the evangelical denominations have influence in the big cities. You also notice a certain prejudice against the Northeast and an underlying ideology that a more modern Brazil would be better off rid of a more backward Brazil. It is a kind of implicit ideology, which sometimes shows up more, sometimes less. As for the concertación: the name came to me because, to build the coalition that sustained him, President Lula made an alliance with sectors of the old Brazilian Social Democracy Party (PSDB). Until 2018, the PSDB had been the main rival of Lula’s Workers’ Party (PT). The current vice president, Geraldo Alckmin, headed the sectors willing to join. The PSDB as a whole has shrunk to a small party, and it stayed neutral: it backed Lula neither in 2022 nor now. But the alliance with Alckmin represented a union with former PSDB sectors willing to form the democratic front. So, as in Chile, the two great adversaries came together: in Chile, the Socialist Party and the Christian Democratic Party; in Brazil, the PT and the PSDB. Along with this party coalition, there was an important class coalition. Lulism represents the base of the Brazilian social pyramid, as everyone knows. But the alliance with this faction of the PSDB also brought in what I call the cosmopolitan bourgeoisie, the most modern sector of the Brazilian bourgeoisie, which backed President Lula in the second round of 2022, not the first. That was very important both for his victory and for the future of the government. In this 2026 election, that sector of the bourgeoisie did not speak out; it stayed neutral and backed neither Flávio Bolsonaro nor President Lula. João Moreira Salles — founder of Piauí magazine, an important filmmaker, and an heir to one of Brazil’s biggest banking families — wrote a very powerful article on the importance of that silence. The consequence of that silence was the acceptance, practically until the last minute, of a Flávio Bolsonaro victory. An extraordinary movement reversed that in this year’s second round. To conclude for now: the cosmopolitan sector of the Brazilian bourgeoisie, which stayed silent, is no longer explicitly present in the concertación. Catarina Príncipe You define Latin American populism as a mass phenomenon: in certain circumstances, classes take the form of multitudes with little or no class organization, connecting people and leader directly. Was this type of populism what secured Lula’s victory? And how can we reconnect this expression of the multitude with more sustained class organization? André Singer I think the concept of populism doesn’t apply to the second-round victory. It’s a very interesting question, and it’s going to give me some work, because I’ll have to develop something more sophisticated to account for the phenomenon. But at first sight, I think we had a social explosion — let’s call it that — without the characteristics of populism. It was more organized and more conscious of its aims than the populist phenomenon implies. To be clear, my theoretical framework is Ernesto Laclau’s old definition, from 1978, not that of the so-called second Laclau. It is a good one for thinking about populism in Latin America and, of course, in Brazil too. Why do I say the explosion is more conscious and more organized? More conscious because it aimed, first, to stop the far right. Flávio Bolsonaro won [the first round] by 2 percentage points and immediately began putting together his government and saying he would change the Constitution. That was a tactical error, even from his own standpoint: it had such an impact that the democratic sectors of Brazilian society immediately began to speak out and organize. That is one side of the phenomena. The other is a feeling that President Lula needed a fourth term, because the government itself began to change during the campaign. It isn’t obvious, but President Lula changed the campaign in mid-September without saying so: he began to take measures. One event seems revealing to me. On September 11, at a rally in Porto Alegre, he said, “I know you are finding products expensive at the supermarket,” referring to coffee and beef. That is very significant, because until then the government had not addressed the population’s material needs directly. From then on, the president not only spoke to those needs but began taking measures. For example, he raised the Bolsa Família benefit, which the government had not adjusted in four years, and he banned online betting, the “bets.” Remember that Brazil is living through a triple crisis: a cost-of-living crisis, a crisis of household indebtedness, and, on top of it, an epidemic of bets. People began gambling wildly, partly to earn extra income to pay off debts. Since betting companies design bets so that the great majority lose, people ended up worse off. President Lula faced great resistance to the ban. First, many companies are involved, and long-term legal contracts were already in place; second, soccer clubs, which are very popular and important in Brazil, depended to some extent on sponsorship from those companies. The other very important decision was the switch from six workdays and one day off (6x1) to five and two (5x2), cutting the workweek from forty-four to forty hours: probably the greatest labor victory since the 1988 Constitution. Congress passed it, but everyone knows it was the president’s initiative and that he committed himself to it. Structurally, of course, it is even more important than the betting ban. But the ban has symbolic meaning, because the president decided on it during the campaign: an act of boldness and courage in defense of the popular economy. Alongside it, the government took two measures to restructure the debts of the popular classes, and others such as free public transit on weekends, which speaks directly to the young people who took to the streets. What I mean is that all this is not populist rhetoric; these are actions. It is what I call a change in the character of the government. Finally, these sectors that took to the streets are not completely disorganized. The demonstrations took place in hundreds of cities, but the largest, and most unprecedented, were in São Paulo, the country’s biggest metropolis. I have been comparing the two October demonstrations in São Paulo, on October 11 and 24, with the great right-wing demonstration for the impeachment of President Dilma Rousseff in March 2016. There had been no demonstration of this kind for at least ten years. The Left led these demonstrations, although they were not only of the Left. They formed a democratic front, with centrist sectors and possibly even a democratic right: individually, people may have gone out to defend democracy. But the leadership clearly belonged to the Left, and these are possibly the largest left-wing demonstrations in Brazil’s history. The Brazilian left has organizations: the PT, the Socialism and Liberty Party (PSOL), the Communist Party of Brazil (PCdoB), the student organizations, the cultural associations, the unions, the neighborhood associations, and the popular movements, especially the Landless Workers’ Movement (MST) and the Homeless Workers’ Movement (MTST). On the center left, you have the Socialist Party of Brazil (PSB) and the Labour Democratic Party (PDT). In short, Brazil has an organizational structure, and it mobilized. So, from these two angles, I wouldn’t describe this as a populist phenomenon; something different happened. Aldo Cordeiro Sauda This year, you observed a pendular movement by the cosmopolitan wing of the bourgeoisie toward the far-right candidacy, the opposite of its support for Lula’s election in 2022. Internationally, US foreign policy shows the same pendular movement: sympathy for Lula under Joe Biden in 2022, explicit support for Bolsonarism under Trump in 2026. To what extent does the Brazilian ruling class’s shift toward Bolsonarism express mere deference to Washington? André Singer As far as I understand, the sector I call cosmopolitan — in the American case, the big technology companies — backed Biden in 2020. In 2024, it wasn’t very clear to me what they were doing, but they didn’t seem to back Trump either, with the exception of Elon Musk. Yet when Trump took office, all of them were there. In the Brazilian case, though, it seems plausible that a conversion of the American cosmopolitan bourgeoisie to the far right influenced the Brazilian bourgeoisie. Until the last minute, there was a certain expectation that this sector might speak out in favor of President Lula. That sector committed itself to democracy in 2022, in a movement broader than support for President Lula. In August 2022, at a demonstration in São Paulo, those business leaders issued a letter. They said they would not accept, under any circumstances, a refusal to recognize the election result — exactly what the White House said. Those two positions were very important in keeping most of the armed forces from joining the coup, because the military knew it could not govern without that support. So you see: there is a Brazilian phenomenon. A link to a transformation in the United States is a possible hypothesis. Catarina Príncipe Our understanding of the question is that the Brazilian cosmopolitan bourgeoisie is staying neutral now because of the political change in the United States from Biden to Trump. At the time of the coup attempt, the Biden presidency was very important in stopping it from going forward. Now, with Trump, there might be some attempt at direct intervention in Brazilian politics. So, part of the cosmopolitan bourgeoisie doesn’t want to take a position today, to avoid a falling-out with US policy and with a possible Bolsonaro victory. It’s less a direct mirror between fractions of the bourgeoisie. André Singer Then I’ll take advantage of your interpretation to add something that makes the problem more complex. The major point of division between that sector of the Brazilian bourgeoisie and Lula’s third government is the fiscal deficit. That sector demands a big cut in public spending, which in its view would have to fall on pension benefits, and it wants to delink them from the minimum wage. The Brazilian Constitution links the two, so raising the minimum wage in real terms also raises all benefits. The other target is the constitutional floor for health and education: the Brazilian Constitution requires that a certain share of annual tax revenue go to health and education, and this cannot go down. The bourgeoisie’s aim is to remove that floor from the Constitution, so that this spending falls. So, we have a very serious issue: on one side the pension system, all the retirees; on the other, the two main social policies that form the social core of the 1988 Constitution, health and education. That is the main problem. We still don’t know whether there is also a certain caution or a desire to align with the American cosmopolitan bourgeoisie. Aldo Cordeiro Sauda National sovereignty took center stage in the campaign, perhaps for the first time since the return to democracy. What role did this issue play in the second-round turnaround against Flávio Bolsonaro? André Singer The Trump administration’s offensive against Brazil — the tariffs and its direct or indirect intervention in the elections — has put national sovereignty on the agenda. Trump justified the first tariffs by saying that Brazil was persecuting his preferred candidate, Jair Bolsonaro. Brazil today does not have a very strong nationalist current. A nationalism is now starting to grow, because the global situation has changed and the country faces political-economic aggression — let’s call it that. So nationalism has come onto the agenda, but in my opinion — and I may be wrong — it has still not become a central issue. Catarina Príncipe Lula wants to transform the Brazilian economy by investing in the green economy, infrastructure, and artificial intelligence (data centers) and by using Brazil’s resources in rare metals and minerals. How much room for maneuver does he have to do this, given the New Fiscal Framework, the Lula government’s 2023 fiscal rule capping annual spending growth at 70 percent of revenue growth? How should we think about his government’s relationship with the bourgeoisie in this fourth term and the new balance of forces? Do you believe the bourgeoisie will tend to deepen its conflict with the PT, intensifying the pendular movement? And in this context, what happens to the mass mobilization from below that we saw in the second round? André Singer I think this is the central point regarding the fourth term: what the outcome of this conflict will be. The stock market fell nearly 14 percent the day after the election. As I have been saying, the market has no vote, but it has money, and its message is clear: if you don’t cut public spending, we’re leaving. The question of fiscal adjustment is truly central, because the bourgeoisie is demanding harsh austerity. In my opinion, the demand for austerity is the fundamental issue in Brazilian politics today, but in general nobody puts it openly: it remains an implicit debate. That is partly because we are not managing to politicize the problem, to make the popular classes, the working class, aware that this is what is at stake. This is the main confrontation. This organizes Brazilian politics. In my recent book, Impasse : O Brasil diante da onda reacionária , I tried to show that this issue splits the democratic front in two. It is, as Americans say, an elephant in the room: everyone treats it as if it didn’t exist. I felt that my role was to bring it to the surface; obviously I can’t do that alone, but I can contribute to some extent. The conflict is immediate, because the transformation Brazil needs, which runs through reindustrialization, is a gigantic task. Brazil is an enormous country, and you don’t change a structure of this order without major investment. This transformation can’t rely on public investment alone; there must also be private investment. But we have to think with the instruments we have. Perry Anderson says Keynesianism no longer works, so we need to create new mechanisms; but until we have them, I’ll use the old ones. The state will have to induce this development process, although it also has to bring in other investors. There is, therefore, an incompatibility between the country’s needs and this radical cut in public spending, which goes in the opposite direction. This is the central point. Even if the terms of the debate were not clear, I think the large demonstrations in hundreds of Brazilian cities point toward the government having this commitment. We’ll have to follow events to see how it unfolds. Catarina Príncipe Your earlier book defined Lulism as “combating poverty without confronting capital.” Can Lulism go beyond itself, and does it want to? Is there room to do so today, given the current party arithmetic in Congress? And how can the Brazilian left organize to force it to take measures that go beyond welfarism? André Singer I’ll start with Congress, which I think is simpler. In the Congress that takes office in 2027, the far right has grown, not at the expense of the Left but of other forces on the Right. In the Chamber of Deputies, it went from 91 to 121 deputies, out of 513 seats. That is significant: since the return to democracy, we would hardly find such a large single-party caucus. But it decides nothing on its own. What we will have is permanent negotiation, which is already happening: Lula’s third government already negotiated permanently with what we in Brazil call the Centrão . To be clear, the Centrão is the established right, the traditional right, so to speak. It generally holds the majority in Brazil’s National Congress, because the Brazilian electoral system reproduces small local oligarchies that tend to dominate legislative elections. This is structural in Brazil, and it will continue. President Lula has specialized in negotiating with those sectors. The third term was the most difficult in this respect, because Congress gained power from what we in Brazil call the “secret budget” ( orçamento secreto ) [budget amendments through which lawmakers steer federal funds without disclosing who requested them]. Even so, the president managed to pass his two boldest proposals. The first was the income-tax exemption for those who earn up to R$5,000 (about US$940) a month, offset by a levy on those who earn more than R$50,000 (about US$9,400). The Chamber of Deputies approved it unanimously. The second was the change of the work schedule from 6x1 to 5x2, which we have already discussed. The Chamber had already approved it unanimously, and the Senate has just passed it by an overwhelming majority. This shows that such negotiation is possible. The traditional right makes concessions on one side and concessions on the other. Its concession to the far right is an effort to reduce the sentences the courts imposed on Jair Bolsonaro and on everyone they convicted of taking part in the 2022 coup attempt, and that effort will expand. It will probably have real consequences: the far right will try to make it possible for Bolsonaro to run in 2030. I think that is its outlook. I repeat, it won’t achieve this without the support of the Right, but depending on the back-and-forth negotiations, it could happen. I now turn to the problem of the Left. The Left should not leave the democratic front. The central problem in Brazil, as in many countries around the world, is to isolate the far right and reverse its advance toward power everywhere. Looking at the long term, we are witnessing a gradual, slow, but constant advance of the far right, sometimes faster, sometimes slower. If the far right comes to power and consolidates itself around the whole world, the working class will suffer a tremendous setback in every respect. Our task, then, is to avoid this by isolating the far right and defeating it as an alternative for power in Brazil. For that, we have to stay in the democratic front. But two incompatible economic programs divide the democratic front. We have to fight explicitly inside this democratic front for our position to win a majority. I’m convinced that democracy depends on the majority of the population recognizing in it an answer to their problems; if it doesn’t, it won’t last. That is the best contribution the Left can and must make to the defense of democracy. Lulism, as I characterized it, is a movement that seeks to combat poverty, which is fundamental in Brazil, without confronting capital. I stand by that definition. But political reality is dynamic. We and all the other actors are facing new situations, so new things are bound to happen. As you know, we can’t predict the future; we can only see tendencies. I would end by saying that a popular commitment is in Lulism’s nature: it depends on a popular base; it is a popular movement. Beyond that, only the political process will tell. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: Equality Is About Who Rules
articles.author: Matt McManus
articles.content: There is a complex debate about the extent to which socialists prioritize equality above the full flowering of each person’s individuality. But you’d have to be quite the contrarian to deny that socialists take equality very seriously; perhaps more seriously than any other major political ideology. Prominent socialist thinkers like G. A. Cohen and Thomas Piketty have dedicated much of their work to defending the philosophical and economic merits of egalitarianism. Socialist Martin Luther King’s “I Have a Dream” speech put equality at the core of his vision: “that one day this nation will rise up and live out the true meaning of its creed: ‘We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal.’” That said, the commitment of socialists and other egalitarians to equality can often seem frustratingly vague. It invites accusations of ill-defined “social justice” advocacy or even pursuing the much dreaded “equality of outcomes” through a Harrison Bergeron–like willingness to cut everyone down to size. Of course, many of these charges are lobbed in bad faith, and even the more refined versions ignore how other core principles — like liberty or order — are equally contestable and vague until explicitly defined. But having a firmer grasp on what we mean by equality and what we want would help the Left understand itself better. Equality of What? Few living thinkers have done more to answer this question than University of Michigan philosopher Elizabeth Anderson. A former doctoral student of John Rawls, Anderson made her name in the 1990s criticizing contemporary egalitarian philosophy and developing her own version of relational equality. More recently, Anderson has become a vigorous proponent of workplace democracy, contending that there is something deeply tyrannical about the forms of work that exist today. Her most recent book , Hijacked: How Neoliberalism Turned the Work Ethic Against Workers and How Workers Can Take It Back , argues for rehabilitating the tradition of social democratic and socialist political thought as a counter to the Right’s moralizing about work. From the beginning, Anderson was fiercely critical of many dimensions of contemporary capitalism and its inequalities. Her early book Value in Ethics and Economics (1993) is a careful critique of how market relations and their distinct ways of reasoning about ethical questions are increasingly colonizing many spheres of society. She insisted that realizing many forms of “freedom, autonomy and welfare demands that certain goods be produced, exchanged, and enjoyed outside of market relations or in accordance with non-market norms.” While in this book Anderson typically appeals to ideas of autonomy and welfare rather than strict equality, there is a clear egalitarian undercurrent. She criticizes libertarians’ “fetishism” of property and markets as the sole site of freedom, and how this leads them to be blind to the “social relations of domination that exist prior to market transactions and that condition the choices individuals make there.” For instance, a long history of patriarchal subordination means that women may feel compelled to enter into exploitative contracts, say, in the sex industry, to get by day to day. In her important paper “What Is the Point of Equality?” Anderson clarifies the role equality plays in inhibiting domination. It opens with a sardonic question: “If much recent academic work defending equality had been secretly penned by conservatives, could the results be any more embarrassing for egalitarians?” She chastises both Marxists like G. A. Cohen for trivializing equality by reducing it to debates about whether we ought to compensate people for being temperamentally gloomy or easily bored, and liberal egalitarians like Ronald Dworkin for proposing an envy-free distribution of resources — implying conservatives are right that the push for equality is ultimately about nothing more than resentment. Anderson wanted egalitarians to finally get serious and realize that we aren’t, in fact, all that interested in building a society where people get the same bundle of goodies. Inegalitarian societies have built hierarchies whose social relations enabled some people to dominate others, often by insisting that those atop the social hierarchy were intrinsically worth more than those at the bottom. Egalitarians, Anderson argued, are fundamentally committed to undoing those forms of social hierarchy that enabled domination and oppression: Egalitarian political movements oppose such hierarchies. They assert the equal moral worth of persons. This assertion does not mean that all have equal virtue or talent. Negatively, the claim repudiates distinctions of moral worth based on birth or social identity — on family membership, inherited social status, race, ethnicity, gender, or genes. There are no natural slaves, plebeians, or aristocrats. Positively, the claim asserts that all competent adults are equally moral agents: everyone equally has the power to develop and exercise moral responsibility, to cooperate with others according to principles of justice, to shape and fulfill a conception of their good. In The Imperative of Integration , Anderson further defined the parameters of what she called the “relational theory” of equality and inequality. It located the “causes of economic, political, and symbolic group inequalities in the relations (processes of interaction) between groups, rather than in the internal characteristics of their members or in cultural differences that exist independently of group interaction.” Anderson emphasizes that in our society what makes people unequal often isn’t intrinsic to them but the result of the social relations in which they are embedded. But to invoke Karl Marx’s language of fetishism, this is very often obscured by ruling ideologies, which redirect the source of inferiority from social relations onto the individuals and groups themselves. Someone sold into slavery is described, in Aristotle’s terms, as a “natural slave” rather than someone who has been trapped in an oppressively hierarchical social system. Moreover, to reinforce hierarchy we often impute still worse forms of inferiority upon those at the base of the pyramid. For instance, when Senator John C. Calhoun called slavery a “positive good” because slaves were racially inferior, and the best thing for everyone was their paternalistic subordination to the superior race. There is a lot to commend in Anderson’s relational equality. It helped steer egalitarians away from arguing about whether people with highfalutin tastes should be supplied with plovers’ eggs and truffle oil and back toward the hierarchies of oppression that it is the Left’s job to confront. If there is a limitation to her approach, it’s an enduring ambiguity about what a flourishing life ought to look like. This is a necessary part of making the case for equality; namely, why and how would people live better lives if they were more equal through being free of domination. Here Marx provides us with a helpful clue in the third volume of Capital , where he posits that under socialism the cooperative development of human powers and capabilities will become an end in itself for the first time, rather than just a means of training more efficient workers. The development of human powers to foster a rich individuality in community with others ought to be on our horizon, and doing so will mean transcending capitalism. The Tyranny of Private Government and the Conservative Work Ethic In her more recent work, Anderson has become one of the sharpest critics of both capitalist practices and ideology. In Private Government , she asks us to imagine “a government that assigns almost everyone a superior whom they must obey.” This government offers routines but no rule of law: orders can be arbitrary, can change without notice, and can’t be appealed. Worst of all, the bosses answer to no one below them. “They are neither elected nor removable by their inferiors.” Most of us, Anderson point out, don’t have to imagine this. It’s what most of us encounter every day when we go to work. And yet, despite the oppression it entails, we are often told that not only is there no alternative, but that such a system is nothing less than freedom itself. Anderson’s point is well taken. If we were told that tomorrow the federal government was going to tell most Americans when to wake up, what they were going to wear, when they could go to the bathroom and eat lunch, how and when they were going to talk to others, there would be riots in the street. Everyone with a “Don’t Tread on Me!” flag would be making liberal use of their Second Amendment rights, Rand Paul would be weeping on live television, and the Daily Wire would proclaim this the Communist States of America. And yet Anderson observes this is the reality for millions of Americans subject to “private government” every day. She rejects the claim that that the modern commercial firm is a realm of individualism, as opposed to the collectivism of the state. Anderson notes that in the “great contest between individualism and collectivism regarding the mode of production, collectivism won, decisively. Nearly all production is undertaken by teams of workers using large, indivisible forms of capital equipment held in common.” Firms are collective enterprises, where the social relations grant capitalists and managers enormous domineering powers at the expense of their workers. She recommends that the way to respond to these forms of domination is to extend the liberal and democratic norms we already apply to statist collectives to private government: allow workers more democratic rights, greater protections, and the right to assemble and check unaccountable private power. In Hjjacked , Anderson examines some of the ideological reasons many on the Right consider this unacceptable. She points out how from the beginning of the modern era there have been fierce debates over the work ethic and who deserved greater power and rewards: workers or capitalists. Anderson shows how socialists and a surprising number of liberals argued a “progressive work ethic” holding that, since workers did most of the work under capitalism, they were getting a raw deal. But they were always confronted by capitalists advocating a “conservative work ethic” that “stressed discipline, frugality, and asceticism for workers, while reaping the lion’s share of productivity gains for themselves in their capacity as capital owners.” The spirit of this conservative ethic was well captured in Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises’s letter to Ayn Rand, congratulating her on the publication of Atlas Shrugged : You have the courage to tell the masses what no politician told them: you are inferior and all the improvements in your conditions which you simply take for granted you owe to the effort of men who are better than you. If this be arrogance, as some of your critics observed, it is still the truth that had to be said in the age of the Welfare State. Anderson thinks that there are several ways we can confront this ideology. One is by reconstructing and re-canonizing the work of socialist and social democratic thinkers who tried to conceive of better ways to organize the economy. Anderson quips that it is “telling that in the history of political thought, no social democrat has been canonized, despite the huge influence of social democracy in many wealthy capitalist countries.” This is something of an exaggeration outside the United States, where left-wing economic thought has gained more traction, but her point still stands. A major goal of left-wing philosophers ought to be reintroducing large numbers of people to the rich and thoughtful tradition of socialist and social democratic thought, to help inspire thinking about where to go in the future. Anderson is esteemed in academic circles but deserves a much wider popular audience. The times are certainly ripe for her message: in his second administration, Donald Trump has gone on a warpath against workers’ rights and needs, making it harder for public sector employees to engage in collective bargaining. Recently, he even went as far as to adopt an explicit “Let them eat cake” attitude toward rising costs to pay for his siege of Iran: “We’re fighting wars. We can’t take care of daycare.” Anderson offers us ways to both criticize these forms of domination and think through how to envision a better future where workers take back the world they built. But above all else, Anderson reminds us that equality is about more than who gets what. Fundamentally, it’s a question of who rules and who is ruled. For most of us, for most of our waking hours, the answer is that the boss rules and we are ruled. Anderson’s work is an invitation to change that answer.
