articles.title: Ok, Now Don’t F**k It Up!
articles.author: Ted Vaill
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. A few days ago, before the Midterm election, I was hoping for, but not really expecting, a Blue Wave. But we now clearly have a Blue Tsunami - Democrats will be in the majority, by a large margin, in both houses of Congress and a have a strong majority of governors, and in all the largest states except Florida. All the “battleground” states now have Democratic governors and the “trifecta” of the governor and both houses of the legislature. There is also a chance that next year the Interstate Compact will become law (it needs passage from states with a total of 48 more electoral votes), and if this happens the 2028 Presidential election will be decided by the U.S. popular vote and not the small state-favoring Electoral College. In 2028, there will be 19 GOP Senate seats up for election, and 15 Democrat seats. Included in the GOP Senators up for reelection (unless they retire) are: Ashley Moody again (who just squeaked through in Florida); Chuck Grassley (who would be over 100 years old at the end of his term if he wins); Cranky Rand Paul; Trumpster Tim Scott; former Majority leader John Thune; and slick Ron Johnson of Wisconsin. Related: My Family Helped Build America: Donald Trump Is Tearing It Apart And a number of the GOP Senators up for reelection in 2018 have shown that they are willing to work with Democrats to get things done. If the Democrats end up winning the seats in Alaska and Mississippi, they would have 56, and would only need 4 Republican Senators to reach a filibuster-free 60 votes. And 2030 is not much better for the GOP in the Senate. In the House, the Democrat majority might even reach 260 next January (218 is a majority).Impeachment only requires a majority in the House, but 67 in the Senate (out of reach unless a number of Republican Senators decide to flush Lame Duck Trump and/or Warmonger Hegseth. Don’t ruin it The Democrats have a history of screwing up a sure thing, by trying to go for too much. Both Clinton and Obama tried to fix the health care system, and the voters punished them in 1994 and 2010.Medicare for all is the right thing to do, but how is it going to be paid for? How do the Democrats fix the economy and healthcare when Trump blew up the national debt to $40 Trillion? Since 2000, our Electoral College-favored GOP Presidents have grossly expanded the debt, leaving it for the Democratic Presidents that follow them to fix the problem. It will happen again in 2028. Related: Trump Denied Project 2025: Now He’s Carrying It Out And then there is 80-year-old and looking unwell and perhaps mentally unstable Trump. What will he do now that the voters have stripped him of much of his power? Bomb-bomb-bomb Iran? Create a Reichstag-like fire to allow him to impose the Insurrection Act on the American people? What will the leaders of the military not fired by Trump choose to do if Trump and Hegseth ask them to follow illegal and unconstitutional orders? What if the Republican leader in the House (possibly current Speaker Johnson, who has chosen not to be the Minority Leader in the next Congress, leaving it to Majority Leader Scalise or Jimmy “I love to wrestle boys” Jordan), try to prevent the seating of new Democratic Congressmembers next January 3? Jordan was deeply in bed with Trump on 1/6/20. Could Trump work with him to create another 1/6 coup to cause chaos as the new Congress is being certified? Many of us who voted for change in the Midterms won’t allow it to happen.

articles.title: Fear of ICE
articles.author: Jeremy Lindenfeld, Reia Li
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Last June, Job Garcia — a U.S. citizen — was tackled to the ground by federal immigration agents while he was filming an ICE raid at a Home Depot in Hollywood. Yesterday, Garcia cast his ballot for the midterm elections at a church less than two miles from where he was arrested, overcoming his fears that ICE agents might show up at the polls. “I’ve been looking forward to this day since what happened to me last year,” said Garcia, 38, who was detained for 25 hours after being arrested last summer. “While there isn’t an ICE policy directly on the ballot … It’s a very intentional vote that I’m making to hopefully shift the power over to individuals that are going to help make those changes [to immigration policy] possible.” The issue of immigration loomed large over yesterday’s elections in Los Angeles — the county with the largest population of foreign-born residents in the country and ground zero for the Trump administration’s ICE crackdown last year. Capital & Main spoke to more than 30 voters at eight polling places in neighborhoods across L.A. County that were hard hit by the immigration crackdown. Some expressed frustration with the cost of living, others were motivated to come to the polls by Proposition 40, a ballot measure aimed at taxing the state’s wealthiest residents, and still others said the hotly contested Los Angeles mayor’s race brought them out to vote. But most voters interviewed mentioned their opposition to President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown as an energizing concern this election season. Some, like Garcia, came out to vote in person in spite of fears that they would encounter ICE agents when they got there. When Garcia arrived at his polling place in East Hollywood after work Tuesday, he was struck by how few voters were lined up compared to what he remembered of previous elections, and was concerned that the Trump administration’s attempts at voter intimidation may have depressed turnout. In the weeks leading up to the election, the administration stepped up immigration enforcement activity across California and launched a sweeping campaign to find evidence of noncitizen voting. Related: When Faith Defies ICE But those aggressive tactics may have backfired. Early voting surged in the state. Turnout in L.A. County for Tuesday’s election outpaced levels reached during the last midterms in 2022, according to the voter data firm Political Data Inc., with some of the biggest increases in areas with large immigrant populations. In the southeast L.A. County city of Bell, where more than 40% of residents are foreign-born, turnout more than doubled , jumping from 16% in 2022 to 33%. A more than doubling of turnout also occurred in Paramount, a city with a sizable Latino immigrant population that was the site of a large militarized presence during last year’s ICE surge. Ballots are still being counted. While there were no verified reports of ICE agents at L.A. voting centers on Tuesday, voters in immigrant communities had reasons to be concerned leading up to Election Day. Trump had refused to rule out deploying ICE agents at polling sites last May, and administration officials had given mixed messages as to whether there would be a federal law enforcement presence at polls. In late October, Department of Homeland Security officials said ICE would not be targeting polling places. Enrique Velázquez, an organizing director at Proyecto Pastoral, a social justice nonprofit in Boyle Heights, wasn’t taking any chances. Early Tuesday morning, before polls had even opened, he huddled with volunteers to prepare for a full day of monitoring ICE activity. Later that morning, the group spread out to three polling stations in Boyle Heights, a heavily Latino neighborhood where ICE reportedly detained a man on Oct. 31 , to monitor any ICE activity. “Remember, we are not there to intervene, just to watch,” Velázquez told the volunteers. “But we will play a different role if la migra shows up — then we’ll activate the rapid response.” Velázquez said the past few days had been quiet, but when he arrived at his monitoring post in front of the East Los Angeles YMCA, he almost immediately received a message about potential ICE activity just a few blocks away. That alert ended up being a false alarm, but the group remained prepared to report any ICE activity to community members and election workers. Election workers and voters in downtown L.A.’s Millennium Biltmore Tower polling station on Election Day. Maria Beltran, who was working at a polling site in Panorama City in the San Fernando Valley and has been a poll worker in L.A. County for over a decade, said this year was the first time she had been equipped with the number of a hotline to call if ICE agents showed up to voting centers. At a voting center in Boyle Heights, 73-year-old Samuel Galván said he was relieved not to see any armed officers at Tenrikyo Church, but pointed to the Trump administration’s lawsuit preemptively challenging a Democratic victory in Alaska’s Senate race as evidence that the federal government was still “trying to suppress our vote.” In California, weeks before the election, the Justice Department sued state and L.A. County officials, attempting to set aside 20,000 of the state’s ballots that the administration claimed may belong to noncitizens. The effort was rejected by a federal judge, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals and the U.S. Supreme Court . Trump said Tuesday night that he would accept the results of the midterm election, which resulted in the Democrats taking back both the House and Senate, helped in part by large leftward swings among Latino voters in states like Texas and Florida. Samuel Galván stands outside Tenrikyo Church, where he cast his midterm election ballot. In Panorama City , one of the neighborhoods hardest hit by ICE raids last year, Crystal Brito, 34, was motivated to vote for the first time after seeing the impacts of immigration enforcement in the neighborhood. “I want to make a difference for the people that can’t vote — uncles, aunts, families,” Brito said. Olga Blanco, 18, had her undocumented family members on her mind when she cast her first ever ballot yesterday. So did Alexa Vasquez, 25, who was worried about her relatives who had curtailed their hours working as street vendors in response to reports last month of the 45-day ICE operation across California. “There’s people who I know and grew up with who have been deported,” Vasquez said. “It’s made it that much more important to come out and vote.” In the San Fernando Valley neighborhood of Van Nuys, Fernando Vasquez, a 55-year-old firefighter, has seen firsthand the impacts of ICE activity in the area, as he’s been called to treat both immigrants and agents who need medical care. But unlike many of the voters Capital & Main interviewed, he supports the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown and he said he hoped for a “Red Wave” this election. Related: The L.A. Nonprofit Where the Formerly Incarcerated Grow Organic Produce “They’re taking care of business. ICE is doing their job,” Vasquez said. That wasn’t the view of Angus Johnson, a 26-year-old who was arrested and sentenced to 14 days in prison for spitting at federal officers during anti-ICE protests last summer. After his arrest, Johnson said he became disillusioned about the effectiveness of electoral politics, but he ultimately came around to the idea of voting. “Nothing has ever been perfect in this country, and it’s nice to hold onto the hope that life will get better,” Johnson said. “I can’t hope for that if I’m not at least doing the one easy little thing I can do to make any sort of difference at all.” Angus Johnson stands in a doorway outside a YMCA in Koreatown where he dropped off his ballot a day early. Garcia had just left his East Hollywood polling place when he heard news of the overwhelming Democratic victories in Senate, House and governor’s races across the country. The rebuke of the Trump administration was somewhat cathartic for Garcia, but he resisted joining in the jubilant chorus of left-leaning voices online. “We’ve been in this boat before. It happened during the midterms in his first administration,” Garcia said, adding that “everyone celebrated” when Democrats won a big majority in the House of Representatives in 2018 only to see Trump win the presidency again in 2024. “I’m hoping [ICE violence] will continue to be at the forefront of people’s minds. I’m hoping that there’s a momentum that will prevent us from getting into a position where this is normal.” Capital & Main Jessica Goodheart contributed to this report.

articles.title: Democrats Won
articles.author: Chuck Yates
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. I was pretty depressed when Donald Trump won a second term in 2024, and Republicans secured control of both houses. I knew life was about to get really awful for a lot of people. But I also knew that it was the midterm election in 2026 would determine just how awful, how depressing. Now that election is over, and the big blue wave the pollsters and pundits promised has washed away the MAGA majority, the United States will be in the care of lawmakers who will prefer principle over party and people over politics—or so we may hope. Here in Idaho, with five Republican voters for every Democrat, it’s no surprise that everything stayed bright red. Republican incumbents were reelected, and voters agreed to amend the state constitution to make English the official language. Somewhat surprisingly, they rejected a proposed constitutional amendment that would have given the legislature exclusive authority to regulate marijuana and other psychoactive substances. Proposition 1, The Reproductive Freedom and Privacy Act, failed, but not spectacularly for this state, where the existing Defense of Life Act prohibits abortion except to save the life of the mother, and in cases of rape and incest, and only in the first trimester. The new law would have retained essentially the same restrictions, but it would have decriminalized both the procedure and the medical professionals who perform it. As it is, Idaho abortion law remains more committed to punishing evildoers than to defending the lives of unborn children. Related: Voting for the Future of America In other words, not much will change here in Idaho. And now that the state’s voters have chosen the Winchester Model 1873 as Idaho’s official state firearm—no kidding—demand for that rifle likely will surge, as Idahoans line up to spend nearly $3700 for the 150th anniversary commemorative edition of “The Gun that Won the West.” They’ll want to add John Wayne’s weapon of choice to their home arsenals, but of course it won’t displace their AR-15s and other military hardware. A true Idaho patriot needs at least one assault rifle. Nationally, though, the possibilities are tantalizing for all who value human dignity and decency. Air Force Major Jason Watson may be vindicated in his call for impeachment, conviction, and removal, even if the military justice system will end his career and probably his personal freedom as well. Major Watson is the poster child for the conflict between obedience and conscience. At the time of his arrest, I wrote, “We need more patriots like Major Jason Watson, willing to serve their country by defying their superiors and falling on their swords to prove their sincerity.” Related: What I Learned in Nagasaki: We Are Not Innocent When We Look Away A less Islamophobic Congress may act to end the pointless and wasteful war with Iran. They may restore sovereignty and self determination to the people of Venezuela. They may even take steps to end the slaughter in Gaza and the West Bank. And immigrants may be able, again, to live without having to worry about roving gangs of ICE and Border Patrol thugs. Who knows? We might even see criminal prosecutions for the members of those gangs who’ve murdered innocent Americans exercising their right to “petition the Government for a redress of grievances.” However, the newly elected Democratic majority won’t take office for another two months. In that interval, Trump and his myrmidons will be able to continue their assault on immigrants, on public and protected lands, on randomly chosen enemies foreign and domestic, on the Constitution and the laws of the land, and on the values that informed those “self evident truths” at the moment of the country’s founding. Unregulated mining, drilling, and logging will continue in former national monuments, in national forests, and on BLM lands. The border wall will continue to grow between the US and Mexico, with bulldozers in national parks and backhoes in cultural and historic sites. Air and water will remain threatened by the pollution of rampant development, and endangered species will continue to live without protection, hunted for trophies and crowded into shrinking habitat by subdivisions and shopping malls. Related: Controlling Unalienable Rights in Idaho The midterm election has given us a genuine hope of seeing that morning in America that Ronald Reagan used to talk about. The United States may soon return to the high ideals of its founding documents. But to honor the metaphor, we have to acknowledge that, despite the faint hint of a coming sunrise, the night is not over yet, and dawn may break over the ruined landscape of a once-proud republic awaiting our commitment to restore it. The hard work has only just begun. As Martin Luther King, Jr. once remarked, “We stand in life at midnight; we are always on the threshold of a new dawn.” And most famously, he said, “I say to you today, my friends, that in spite of the difficulties and frustrations of the moment, I still have a dream.” We must resolve to dream with him, and to hold fiercely to that hope.

articles.title: Working-Class Democratic Candidates Won Big in the Midterms
articles.author: Jared Abbott
articles.content: In January, a logger from Maine’s North Woods will take a seat in the US Senate. Troy Jackson spent his adult life cutting timber before he ran for office, and he will be the only Senate Democrat whose working life before politics was spent mostly in a working-class job. But he won’t be alone on Capitol Hill. Across the House, a union ironworker from suburban Cleveland, a Bethlehem firefighter, a Wisconsin waitress, an emergency room nurse, a Montana smoke jumper, a Rochester math teacher, and a former Trader Joe’s worker from Queens are heading to Washington too. By my count, twenty-one Democrats in the next Congress will have spent at least half of their working lives before politics in working-class jobs. Today there are just twelve. Working-class Democrats will still represent a woefully small fraction of the party caucus in the new year, but the 2026 midterms have swelled their ranks fast, and that gives them a real opportunity to come together to lead on a pro-worker agenda. Having more workers in Congress isn’t just a matter of symbolism; it can meaningfully change what government does and how ordinary people feel about their elected officials. Political scientists Nicholas Carnes and Noam Lupu have shown that when workers don’t hold office, economic policy tilts toward the haves and away from the have-nots. Their work demonstrates that when working-class people are underrepresented in office, legislatures are less likely to pass pro-worker policies, governments tend to build less generous welfare states, and citizens have lower trust in their elected officials. A Working-Class Wave Of the over 250 Democrats serving in the current Congress (counting both the House and the Senate), just twelve (4.6 percent) spent most of their pre-political careers in working-class jobs. Meanwhile, roughly half of American workers hold working-class jobs. I count a member of Congress as working class only if they spent at least half of their working life in working-class jobs before entering public office. That means jobs like factory work, waiting tables, office support, teaching, nursing, firefighting, and enlisted military service. A summer job or a few years of college shifts doesn’t count. That rules out many Democrats with real but limited working-class history, whose time in those jobs was too short or too uncertain to count. The ten newcomers who clear that working-class bar mostly won hard-fought, highly competitive races. Indeed, nine of them won or lead in still-uncounted races for seats that Republicans hold today: Brian Poindexter in Ohio’s 7th District; Bob Brooks and Bob Harvie in two Pennsylvania districts; Rebecca Cooke in western Wisconsin; Mitchell Berman in southern Wisconsin; and JoAnna Mendoza, Jake Johnson, and Sam Forstag lead in Arizona, Minnesota, and Montana, respectively. Troy Jackson took a Republican-held Senate seat in Maine. The tenth, Claire Valdez, won an open seat in Brooklyn and Queens, one of the most heavily Democratic districts in the country. These candidates’ résumés read like a cross section of the American working class: Member-elect Seat Before politics Troy Jackson Maine Senate Logger Brian Poindexter Ohio 7th Union ironworker Bob Brooks Pennsylvania 7th Firefighter; beer-truck driver Bob Harvie Pennsylvania 1st High school teacher Rebecca Cooke Wisconsin 3rd Waitress JoAnna Mendoza Arizona 6th Enlisted Navy and Marine Corps Jake Johnson Minnesota 1st Public school math teacher Mitchell Berman Wisconsin 1st Nursing assistant, then nurse Sam Forstag Montana 1st Wildland firefighter Claire Valdez New York 7th Service worker; university administrative assistant Many of these working-class candidates are also union members, and several have held union office: Poindexter as an organizer and apprenticeship instructor, Brooks as president of Pennsylvania’s firefighters’ union, Forstag as a vice president of his Forest Service local, and Valdez as a unit chair in the United Auto Workers. They join eleven returning members with similar backgrounds, from Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the former bartender, to Stephen Lynch, the ironworker who ran his union local, and Norma Torres, a former 911 dispatcher. Working-Class Democrats Span Every Wing of the Party The working-class Democrats come from a wide range of the party’s caucuses. Among current members, they include Congressional Progressive Caucus stalwarts like Ocasio-Cortez and Maxine Waters, New Democrats like Lucy McBath and John Mannion, and Blue Dog Jared Golden. The incoming class is just as mixed. Valdez was backed by Justice Democrats and the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). Jackson was Bernie Sanders’s pick. Harvie was endorsed by the New Democrats’ PAC, Johnson and Berman by both the New Democrats and the Blue Dogs. And Poindexter, Brooks, and Forstag managed something that should be impossible under the party’s factional logic: they were endorsed by both the Progressive Caucus PAC and the Blue Dog PAC. But despite their ideological range, this crop of new working-class Democrats is more progressive on economics than it might at first appear. When I coded the campaign positions of the nine newcomers who ran in swing seats, five came out progressive or leaning progressive, including three the Blue Dogs endorsed. Troy Jackson and Bob Brooks both ran on Medicare for All. Sam Forstag proposed a 5 percent wealth tax on fortunes over $1 billion, Bob Harvie backs the PRO Act and a $15 federal minimum wage, and Brian Poindexter wants to make it easier to join a union and to make the wealthy pay their fair share to shore up Social Security funding. Claire Valdez, who ran in a safe seat in New York City, made Medicare for All one of her three platform pillars, alongside “unions for all” and “housing for all.” Even the newcomers who lean moderate or show no clear lean hold robust pro-worker positions. Rebecca Cooke supports a $15 minimum wage and expanding Medicare to cover dental, vision, and hearing. Mitchell Berman calls for a living wage of about $21.54 an hour and joined striking nurses on the picket line. Jake Johnson wants a new top tax bracket for the highest earners and to break up big corporations that exploit workers. JoAnna Mendoza backs the right to unionize and expanding Medicare as well. Whatever wing of the party they come from, this group’s shared working-class background grounds them in the bread-and-butter, kitchen-table issues that working people care about most and makes them ideal tribunes for working people’s interests on a national stage. They share an experience: of hourly pay, of shift work, of what a health insurance deductible means when you’re living paycheck to paycheck, and of the value of a union contract to families’ financial stability. We Need a Working-Class Caucus in Congress Congress has caucuses for nearly every region, industry, and ideological tendency. The Democrats’ main ideological blocs in the House are the Progressive Caucus, the New Democrat Coalition and the Blue Dogs. But Congress doesn’t have a caucus by and for working people, dedicated purely to delivering material gains that improve the lives of ordinary Americans. The Labor Caucus does important work championing workers’ rights on the job and the priorities of the labor movement, from the PRO Act to a higher minimum wage. A working-class caucus would build on that work with a broader vision: raising the standard of living for all working people and making sure every working family has what it takes to thrive. Such a caucus, of course, wouldn’t need to police who does or doesn’t count as working class, but lawmakers with strong working-class backgrounds, who know firsthand the pressures that working families face, would play a central role. That would give working people not only allies in Congress but a voice of their own. A working-class caucus could do things the existing ones cannot. To start, because working-class lawmakers already sit in caucuses across the party’s ideological spectrum, a working-class caucus could build coalitions across factional lines on bread-and-butter issues like wages, labor law, health care costs, and housing. Each faction supports progress on many of these issues in principle, but an organized bloc would be better placed to push back when party leaders are tempted to let those priorities slide down the agenda. Nick French has made a similar case for the record number of socialists heading to Congress: even a small minority can exert meaningful leverage when it organizes as a bloc. Second, the issues that shape working people’s daily lives would sit at the top of the caucus’s agenda: making sure a full-time job pays enough to support a family; bringing down the cost of housing, health care, and childcare; protecting retirement security; strengthening workers’ right to organize; and investing in the towns and regions that decades of bad economic policy have left behind. Finally, there is the bench of future working-class candidates to build. The 2026 results showed that working-class Democrats can win the competitive seats that decide control of the House, and a caucus could recruit, train, and fund more of them, so that a waitress or an electrician thinking about running knows there is a bloc in Washington that wants her to be there. Organizing twenty or so working-class members of Congress into an organized caucus obviously won’t remake the Democratic Party into a party of the working class on its own. It can’t fix the deeper problem that working people have too little organized power in American politics. But it would give workers more leverage inside the party, because an organized group of pro-worker champions in strategic positions across the party can keep its leadership focused on working people’s priorities and hold the party brass accountable when it strays. articles.title: Steward’s Corner: Rethink the Scripted ‘Ask’
articles.author: Ellen David Friedman
articles.content: You’re having a conversation with a co-worker, but inside you’re feeling icy dread. You’re talking through a script that ends with asking them to do a specific thing: sign a union card, wear a button, come to a meeting, vote for a strike. And sure enough, when you ask, a wall comes down. The co-worker looks away, makes an excuse, and pins you as someone who is after something. You’re disappointed, confused about why it didn’t work, and afraid you’re not going to meet your goal. Many of us feel nervous or awkward about asking a co-worker to do something. Sometimes we just need to push ourselves to do it. But if you’re being pressured to follow the script and get to a particular “ask” without finding out who this person is and moving at their pace, that’s a problem. A co-worker you don’t yet have much of a relationship with may be turned off that you’re pressuring them to take an action that has already been decided on by others. What can you do instead? Replace the “ask” (to take some predetermined action) with an invitation: “Hey, some of us are getting together to talk about this. You want to join us?” “Can we figure out how you can be part of the solution to this problem that you’re posing?” People are happy to be asked to do something they want to do, or that they’re good at, or that they’re confident about. People like to be asked to do things when it reflects your respect for them: “You’re asking me to do this because you’re confident in my ability. You know I like this task, or that I’m good at it.” Think how different that is from simply complying with what the organizer wants them to do. A NEW APPROACH A young worker in a chemical factory in Massachusetts was trying to interest his co-workers in a union. After many frustrating weeks of trying to approach people with an ask—to come to a meeting with a union organizer—he was about to give up. But then he opened his eyes to other possibilities and changed his approach: “What I’m really trying to do is build real relationships,” he said. “I decided to see what happened if I gave up the ask.” With this new approach, in a matter of just two or three weeks, he met his goal to connect with co-workers in a dozen departments where he had not previously had any contact. He found that it was so much easier to make contact when that was the only goal. What had been holding him back from contacting these people before? “I didn’t know what the ask was. And what do they owe me? They’re going to feel bad if they don’t do what I ask. They might avoid me.” TRUST TAKES TIME Instead, his co-workers started to approach him with questions, concerns, and ideas about workplace problems. It emerged that the boss was providing very different retirement packages to different employees. Pretty soon a group came together to document the problem, propose a fix, and bring it to the boss. Of course organizers are asking people to do things all the time—our organizing is about action, not just talk. And there are times when making a specific ask, even pushing hard, makes sense—asking people to commit to a strike, for instance, or to vote yes to join the union. But such urgency should be grounded in strong relationships and discussions that have built trust over time, helping people overcome fear. Any hard “ask” should stem from inclusive discussion and collective decisions. People should be coming up to you to say, “Is that petition what I think it is? Give me that, I want to sign it.” [Do you have a different take on "the ask" or the organizing conversation? Write to editors[at]labornotes[dot]org ] Excerpted from Keep Going: A Guide to Organizing When It’s Hard by Ellen David Friedman, a retired organizer for Vermont NEA and a member of the Labor Notes board.

articles.title: Trump Hurt Average Americans, So They Voted Against the GOP
articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content: You didn’t even have to look at the numbers on Wednesday to know the election was a rout. You could have just guessed it by the fact that Donald Trump didn’t deny the results, call the whole thing “rigged,” or vow to fight the cheaters to the bitter end. Instead he meekly congratulated the Democrats, insisted none of it was his fault, and offered to work with his opposition before getting back to the truly important work of his ballroom . In a two-week period that saw right-wing leaders across the world refuse to concede and try to find ways to deny election results, Trump, the man who first gave them the playbook to do it, was the only one to accept his defeat. It’s a measure not of any change in the president but of how emphatically he was rejected by the country. By now, everyone knows this past Tuesday was a generational calamity for Republicans, and the party is of course now yelling over each other to explain what went so badly wrong. “We forgot that we’re a populist party,” one GOP operative told Politico about the party’s lack of an affordability message. “President Trump’s message won. Unfortunately he wasn’t the messenger,” Trump’s former campaign deputy communications director told Fox News, complaining that his team had “allowed his winning message in 2024 to be co-opted by his opposition.” The issue was just that the GOP “forgot how to win,” wrote outgoing Texas Sen. John Cornyn, blaming the poor “character and integrity” of its candidates and urging the party to be more “likeable.” For Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, now eagerly positioning himself as captain of this shipwreck, the problem was that Republicans were too obsessed with fighting “wokeness,” which was “yesterday’s battle.” It’s not surprising that a party that would allow itself to get destroyed so thoroughly would in the aftermath still be completely oblivious about why they lost. Technically, yes, it was many of these things: the lack of populism, the bad candidates, the ignoring of affordability, the obsession with wokeness. But that’s really underselling it. The reason the Republicans have been decimated is that the party did everything they could possibly do to make almost everyone in the country’s lives dramatically worse for the past twenty-two months: it pushed four hundred thousand people out of their jobs, it is throwing millions of people off of their health care, it wrenched Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits — also known as food stamps — from 5.5 million people, and raised their insurance premiums by 26 percent , with another 13 percent to come next year. This was part of the party’s genius idea of slashing federal support for health care more than anyone had ever done in US history, to the tune of $1 trillion . This is all before you factor in the average of $471 per person in fuel costs alone added to US households’ expenses by the Iran war and the $1,745 more per family they’ve had to pay because of Trump’s blanket tariffs. Mind you, all this was as Trump and the GOP shoveled a trillion dollars in tax cuts — the same amount they had cut from most people’s health care — to the top 1 percent, in a cut that gave 70 percent of its benefits to the wealthiest fifth of Americans. At the same time, it presided over record-high wage theft by employers and actively decided to let hundreds of corporate crooks who gave money to Trump off the hook for a variety of alleged wrongdoing, including price-fixing, workplace discrimination, and forced labor — all while the president and his family lined their own pockets in a way that’s never been seen before in US (or really, human) history, with the president alone growing his net worth by $3 billion through crypto scams that tricked his own voters into buying and being stuck with worthless Trump-themed digital currency. We’re not even getting into the way Trump’s deportation crusade has caused terror, havoc, and death even among US citizens while directly hurting the farming communities that had lent him their support. You will note the problem here is not that Trump and the Republicans were not talking about affordability. Trump could have spent the final weeks of the campaign actually talking about the high cost of living instead of droning on about his reflecting pool and men’s asses , and the reality is people’s lives still would have been significantly, materially worse off because of the policies they sunk untold months, energy, and political capital into to pursue — the same decidedly anti-populist policies Republicans have pushed for decades. Those policies are not the ones desired by ordinary Trump voters, who — if you look at polling and the election results for ballot measures and candidates — want things like a higher minimum wage, a clampdown on price gouging, affordable childcare, and more generous employer benefits. Instead they got the bog-standard neoliberal agenda that the GOP’s donors and corporate sponsors promote, lobby for, and force onto the legislative agenda, because it benefits their bottom lines. It’s not that Republicans suddenly forgot to be populist going into the election. It’s that they had nothing to be populist about . The problem for the GOP here is the same one that the similarly corporate-backed Democratic Party has been wrestling with for decades: the interests of its working-class voters are fundamentally at odds with the interests of the people who fund its campaigns, who bankroll the think tanks they rely on for their policy ideas, and who are often the 1 percenters who make up its roster of elected officials. The Democratic Party is, thanks to the left insurgency in its ranks, currently in the middle of a battle to try and resolve that contradiction. The GOP appears completely oblivious that that contradiction even exists — and as a result, has no real idea why voters just gave it a historic rebuke. articles.title: The Steel Disaster in Taranto, Italy, Is a Warning to Europe
articles.author: Valentin Vogl
articles.content: For decades, labor unions and residents of the southern Italian city of Taranto have been mobilizing around the toxic emissions churned out by the local steel mill. A dedicated group fought for their right to good health through a yearslong legal battle that reached all the way to Italy’s top court. On October 29, the court finally ruled: the blast furnaces, which for decades have blanketed Taranto with fine particulate matter, dioxins, benzene, and asbestos emissions, must close with immediate effect. It represents a bitter-tasting victory after one of the great struggles of European industrial history. ILVA, as Europe’s nominally largest steel mill is still called, stands right in the center of Taranto, a city with a population of nearly two hundred thousand. The steel mill was built in the 1960s, when Italy’s capitalist class dreamed of finally industrializing the South of the peninsula. The company is now called Acciaierie d’Italia (“Italy’s Steelworks”) and has been operating under state-imposed emergency measures since 2024. The history of ILVA is one of Europe’s biggest environmental scandals. Local residents, unions, the mayor, and even the local soccer club have all demanded the closure of the blast furnaces. These efforts have consistently failed for want of government plans for financing alternatives. In statistical terms, the people of Taranto suffer from pleural mesothelioma (a cancer caused by asbestos exposure) four times as much as the general population. In addition, the steel mill has been proven to cause elevated levels of particulate matter and emissions of micropollutants such as benzopyrene and dioxins, as determined by official health-impact assessments. Fans of the local Taranto soccer club have also been fighting against the plant for many years. They have written books, sold scarves with slogans such as “Fabbrica assassina, vergogna tarantina” (“Murderous factory, Taranto’s shame”), and rented public ad space to express their discontent. With the abrupt closure of its largest employer, Taranto faces the threat of social crisis. More than ten thousand jobs depend on the steel mill; enormous health care costs and the cleanup of a toxic wasteland are deterring investors. The situation is fertile ground for the authoritarian right and its ability to turn disappointment, uncertainty, and frustration into votes. The much-heralded return of European industrial policy also bears responsibility for ILVA’s demise. In recent years, governments around Western Europe tried to coax “green” investments out of private capital through generous handouts. And yet, oligarchs and steel tycoons were in no hurry to comply. Although the plant is currently state owned, the government has no concrete plan for continuing production. The site’s future appears to be a painful choice between a complete sell-off to oligarchs or else outright collapse. Europe’s Rusty Steel Empire In an age of (sort of) flying cars, steel mills seem like relics from a bygone era. Appearances are not deceiving. The blast furnace process, used worldwide to produce steel for infrastructure, buildings, cars, and weapons, was developed in China over two thousand years ago. Steel truly took off thanks to the self-accelerating economic model of fossil capitalism : machines needed steel and coal; growing coal mining required more machines; and these, in turn, required more steel and coal. Today’s imperial core then began burning ever more fossil coal in ever-larger blast furnaces to produce pig iron — and greenhouse gases, too. Starting in the 1970s, Europe lost ground to Japan’s rising steel power. Japanese steelmakers dared to build blast furnaces of unprecedented size and, in the process, created a global market for fossil metallurgical coal. Today more than one billion metric tons of coal are burned annually to produce steel. This makes the global steel industry responsible for one-tenth of all human-caused greenhouse gases, more than the EU as a whole. By the time they were privatized in the late 1980s and early ’90s, European steelmakers were already lagging behind the competition, particularly their Japanese rivals. Global steel tycoons also took advantage of the wave of privatizations to snap up plants that were being sold off at bargain prices following the collapse of the Soviet Union. They downsized the plants’ workforces, established companies in tax havens, closed unprofitable sites, and generally generated good returns for themselves and minority shareholders. Today Europe’s steel mills are outdated. No new blast furnace plants have been built since the 1970s, and only two blast furnaces have opened in the EU since 2000. From Eisenhüttenstadt to Fos-sur-Mer, Gijón, Kraków, IJmuiden, and Taranto, in a long list of former steel hubs, local residents suffer from air pollution and health problems. Investments to modernize these facilities and curb emissions are long overdue. Derisking Has Failed In Italy, at the height of the European Green Deal investment projects in the early 2020s, the prime minister was none other than Mario Draghi. He had previously been a key figure at Goldman Sachs and, as president of the European Central Bank throughout the 2010s euro crisis, a key figure in the troika that imposed austerity on the Greek government. Since 2024, Draghi’s name has come to symbolize EU competitiveness and the associated watering down of European environmental and human rights policies. In the meantime, in 2021–22, Draghi served as Italian premier and developed a climate road map for the steel plant in Taranto. Beginning in 2019, Europe’s steel manufacturers successively announced decarbonization plans to transition from coal to hydrogen and electric furnaces in order to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. In Taranto, according to Draghi’s plan, €4.7 billion in largely private capital was to be invested to achieve full employment and increase production by 2025. The political ideology in which economic policy levers are adjusted so that unattractive investments like “green steel” become viable business cases is called “derisking.” The European Green Deal aims to make the steel industry climate neutral and competitive again through such means. Specifically, this meant free emissions allowances, billions in state aid for steel and hydrogen, protective tariffs against China, public procurement of “green steel,” energy price subsidies, and more lenient reporting requirements. In an attempt to make green investments attractive to private capital, several EU countries dealt with ArcelorMittal. The world’s second-largest steel company holds a de facto monopoly on blast furnace production in Spain, France, Belgium, and Poland and operates additional blast furnaces in Germany (Bremen and Eisenhüttenstadt). From 2018 to 2024, ArcelorMittal also operated the plant in Taranto. Yet governments underestimated the steel giant’s negotiating position; it abruptly announced that it could not invest at all locations, thereby provoking a subsidy race among member states. Up to €15 billion in low-carbon subsidies has since been awarded to steelmakers, but even that is not enough. As a result of high energy prices following the invasion of Ukraine, ArcelorMittal put all hydrogen projects on hold at the end of 2024. Seven lost years after the Green Deal, only a few Swedish and German steelmakers in the EU are still pursuing significant decarbonization projects. Meanwhile, many locations are in an even worse economic position than before. The EU’s “derisking” project appears to have failed, at least for now. Draghi is quite right to blame the industry’s struggles to a lack of competitiveness. Raw materials and energy mostly have to be imported. Labor costs are comparatively high due to Europe’s past imperial might but also its historic labor struggles. Europe’s historical advantage in innovation has long since been squandered; the innovation hubs of the steel industry are now in Japan, Korea, and above all China. Added to this are persistent global overcapacity and higher returns in the financial sector, which is why ArcelorMittal prefers to carry out share buyback programs rather than make forward-looking investments. Yet instead of EU member states pursuing alternative and more democratic economic models, the lack of competitiveness serves as a pretext to pursue austerity measures and the upward redistribution of wealth. Europe’s steel-producing regions are thus kept in a state of perpetual crisis, which further exacerbates health and climate damage. The authoritarian right skillfully exploits the resulting uncertainty about people’s jobs and the economic survival of their hometowns. This too is a result of timid industrial policies. In turn, these same right-wing parties, building on neoliberal ideological assumptions, further undermine democracy. Socialization Is Not Enough A bold democratic alternative is urgently needed to ensure a stable supply of raw materials. The good news is that we’re not starting from scratch. In June, the French National Assembly voted for the second time to nationalize the French division of ArcelorMittal, but the measure has so far failed to gain Senate approval. In Germany, in a recent position paper, Die Linke advocates for state involvement in the steel industry. Some steel manufacturers, such as the German companies Saarstahl and Salzgitter, are either part-publicly owned or bound to social interests. In Austria, Voestalpine employees own 15 percent of the company. Recent developments in France and Germany make it clear that momentum is finally building around the issue of ecosocialist industrial policy. Yet socialist parties are running late, and nationalization alone is not enough. Rather, the direction of these plants must be anchored in a solid transformation strategy. Democratic management of industry requires that we wrest the systems of provision we need to meet our basic needs from the logic of capital accumulation. Such transformative supply systems must be protected from capital and structured in such a way that social participation has a self-accelerating effect. This presents two fundamental challenges for the democratization of the steel industry. First, solutions are needed to protect socialized steel mills from the capitalist market. Only in this way can economic leeway be created for radical experiments in Europe’s outdated and contaminated facilities. Long-term offtake agreements with public infrastructure operators (such as water or energy utilities) could be a first step. Further socialization of major steel consumers could be the next. The second is that the EU obtains most of its energy and raw materials through imports. Dependence on raw materials makes socialist experiments vulnerable to crisis-induced market fluctuations and acts of economic sabotage. Increased use of scrap steel and renewable energy within the EU can mitigate these risks. In the spirit of “resilience by cooperation,” solidarity-based alliances can be built beyond the EU, with the goal of dismantling colonial patterns in value chains and organizing the procurement of more socially and environmentally sustainable primary raw materials in the longer term. In Taranto, the state and private capital are leaving behind a toxic wasteland that hangs over the future generations. Even beyond the enormous costs of repairing this situation, hopes of industrial transformation are also complicated by the presence of organized crime in every stage of the waste cycle and its frequent involvement in public-procured construction projects, as documented by Italian NGO Legambiente in its No Ecomafia campaign. Given these obstacles, democratizing production is likely the only way for Taranto to retain the site in the long term. Unions and the local population have already mobilized and have the only concrete plan for the plant’s future. For the rest of Europe, Taranto remains a cautionary tale: a foretaste of what might come next. articles.title: Palestinians Beat Israel's Political System
articles.author: Ramzy Baroud
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The results of Israel’s Oct. 27 election have been welcomed by Palestinian communities in Israel and worldwide. Neither the right-wing bloc of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor that of his rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, secured the 61 seats required to form a government. This made the 19 seats won by Palestinian parties all the more consequential. Related: Netanyahu or Not, Israel's Occupation of Palestine Will Continue In a political system structured to marginalize its Palestinian minority, the electoral achievement of the Joint List and Ra’am cannot be overstated. Through their relative unity and an extraordinary convergence of political circumstances, Palestinian voters have seemingly managed to beat the system. This achievement came despite fearmongering and outright racist rhetoric by the mainstream Jewish political parties and their leaders, including Eisenkot. Netanyahu built much of his campaign on the specter of a Palestinian political takeover. On election day, he warned : “If we don’t wake up now, we’ll find ourselves with a government of Mansour Abbas and Ahmad Tibi.” While presenting itself as democratic, Israel has waged political, legal and constitutional wars against its Palestinian citizens Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir employed similar rhetoric. Alarmed by Palestinian turnout, he declared : “If you want this country to stay Jewish and Zionist … go out and vote.” He also warned his supporters: “Don’t let them win.” Even Eisenkot, often portrayed in Western media as a more amiable and less hawkish alternative to Netanyahu, rejected the prospect of governing with the Palestinian parties, declaring : “I do not see an Arab party that accepts my principles.” Whether the electoral deadlock forces him to reconsider that position is another matter. The point is that Eisenkot and his potential allies, including Naftali Bennett and Yisrael Beiteinu leader Avigdor Lieberman, have rejected Palestinian participation in any governing coalition. Imagine this happening in a true democracy: an entire political community excluded from government because its members are Black, Irish or Christian, for example. This is the crux of Israel’s democracy problem. While presenting itself as democratic, Israel has waged political, legal and constitutional wars against its Palestinian citizens, treating their very identity as a threat to the Jewish character of the state. Historically, this has been the central point of contention among Palestinian communities in Israel: Why should Arabs participate in elections that validate a system constructed, from its foundation, to entrench Jewish supremacy and persecute its Palestinian minority? History occasionally produces moments so dangerous that even morally defensible positions must be reconsidered Consider the Knesset itself. Section 7A of its Basic Law allows electoral lists and candidates to be disqualified for rejecting Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state. Imagine Black American politicians being required to recognize the US as a white nation before being permitted to contest elections. In 2018, Israel went further, passing the Nation-State Basic Law, which declares that the right to national self-determination in Israel is “unique to the Jewish people.” It is therefore hardly surprising that some Palestinian political movements have refused to participate in what they regard as a political charade, choosing instead to defend their communities’ rights outside of a fundamentally rigged parliamentary system. One example is Abnaa Al-Balad, which has long advocated boycotting Knesset elections rather than granting legitimacy to the Israeli political order. This debate resembles the historical disagreement between revolutionary abstentionism, which rejects participation in institutions deemed illegitimate, and socialist parliamentary participation, which argues that refusing parliamentary engagement should not become an absolute principle. Israel’s latest election has given this debate renewed urgency. To be clear, although some Arab parties have roots in leftist traditions, none can simply be described as revolutionary. Related: Empty Stadiums, No Accountability: Israel and the Sports Boycott Ra’am, led by Mansour Abbas, participated in the Zionist coalition government formed by Bennett and Yair Lapid in June 2021. Abbas effectively sidelined broader Palestinian national aspirations in favor of municipal budgets, socioeconomic equality and combating crime within Palestinian communities in Israel. Ra’am last week won eight seats and Abbas has made clear his willingness to pursue the same strategy. The Joint List, meanwhile, secured 11 seats. Its priorities include removing Netanyahu, defending Palestinian national rights and advancing social justice for the Palestinian citizens of Israel. Now, more than ever, Palestinians need unity. All are facing extraordinary threats: the ongoing genocide in Gaza, accelerating annexation and ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, and further suppression of Palestinian communities inside Israel. By uniting around a political program capable of defeating Netanyahu’s far-right agenda and setting aside their factional interests, Arab politicians could achieve something their previous parliamentary efforts failed to accomplish: they could force Israel to change direction, slow its machinery of death and remove Netanyahu, who is wanted on war crimes charges, from power. While one may insist, on principle, that participating in a corrupt political system validates that very system, history occasionally produces moments so dangerous that even such morally defensible positions must be reconsidered, however temporarily. The choice now is not between purity and betrayal but between paralysis, allowing Netanyahu’s wars to continue unchecked, and strategic disruption. Certain distinctions, however, must remain absolutely clear. Replacing Netanyahu is not liberation. Eisenkot is no peacemaker — he is a committed Zionist whose military record and political positions offer Palestinians little reason to expect justice. A new Israeli government will not erase the crimes of the state or fundamentally dismantle its apartheid system. What such a change might offer, however, is a disruption of the alliance through which Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich have pursued their agenda of genocide, ethnic cleansing and annexation, potentially slowing Israel’s capacity to inflict violence on the current scale. Real change, on the other hand, can only be achieved through genuine Palestinian unity and resistance on all fronts, sustained global solidarity, legal accountability and meaningful political action. articles.title: Coolers
articles.author: William J. Astore
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. A favorite movie of mine is “ The Cooler ,” starring William H. Macy. Macy plays a sad sack, a loser, a guy down at the mouth and down on his luck. He’s employed as a “cooler” at a casino. Whenever someone is winning too much at the roulette wheel or at craps, Macy goes and stands near the high-rolling winner. Within moments, the high-roller starts to lose, and lose big. Macy is good at his job. Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer are the Democratic Party’s coolers. They’re being sent in by the house (the owners and donors in America’s casino-style capitalism) to cool any real change that might hurt the bottom line of the rich. And they’re good at their jobs. Another “cooler” is the “liberal” New York Times . I caught this summary this morning of the Democratic Party’s goals come next year: Related: When Everything Is Political, What Happens to Art? Congress. Chuck Schumer, the likely Senate majority leader, says job No. 1 is to bring down the cost of living for Americans. Democrats want to reverse Medicaid cuts, restore Obamacare subsidies, limit Trump’s ability to impose tariffs and curtail a war that has raised fuel costs. Trump promises he can be “Mr. Veto” if necessary. Even so, Democrats can force his allies into votes they’ll regret when the next election comes around. Democrats also want to exercise their constitutional power to check the executive branch and conduct oversight. Now they promise to investigate crypto windfalls, well-timed stock trades and a wedding party for the president’s son bankrolled by a Kremlin-connected oligarch. One House Democrat said in a statement on Tuesday that White House officials should “lawyer up.” Cooler, indeed. Basically, it’s a return to the Biden status quo. I like the part about curtailing a war that has raised fuel costs. Is that the worst part of the Iran War—that it’s raised fuel costs? And why “curtail” instead of ending the war? Isn’t the war illegal, immoral, unconstitutional, and disastrous? Also, I like the part about going after Trump and his family for profiting from insider trading and the like. Speaking of that, Nancy Pelosi and many other leading Democrats should also “lawyer up.” Related: Trump's One-Man Horror Show Continues Of course, you’ll notice what isn’t mentioned by these coolers. There’s nothing about raising the minimum wage, nothing about single-payer health care, nothing about ending wars globally, nothing about major cuts to spending on wasteful wars and obsolete weaponry, and most certainly nothing about cutting weapons and other “aid” to Israel as it pursues a genocide in Gaza. Among rank-and-file Democrats at the moment, there’s a lot of positive energy. A lot of high hopes for real and substantive changes. But the house has already taken action—it’s sending in the coolers, because the little guy and gal can’t be allowed to win when those wins hurt the bottom line of the owners. Bracing Views

articles.title: Chapter Notes: November 2026
articles.author: Pinellas DSA
articles.content: Hello again, comrade! It’s the November edition of the Pinellas DSA Chapter Notes! We know that you’re probably still processing the results from the election on Tuesday. A lot of the votes in which we were most invested, like Angie’s campaign for US Senate and Amendment 3 to the state constitution, didn’t go our way. And, Florida is in for another four years of the reactionary Republican leadership in Tallahassee. But it’s not all bad news. In fact… far from it . Pinellas DSA members watch as election results trickle in on November 3. Pinellas DSA member Lindsey Grove won her bid for St. Pete City Council District 6, meaning a quarter of the council is now in DSA hands for the next four years! Our Tampa DSA comrade Ashley Herrmann won her race for Florida House District 69, flipping the seat from Republican Danny Alvarez. Republicans lost 15 seats, as well as their supermajority, in the Florida State House. And, DSA-endorsed candidates won key races across the country, including Melat Kiros in Colorado, Rashida Tlaib and Donavan Mckinney in Michigan, Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania, and more. Even in defeat, we can point to the fact that Angie shocked all the pollsters and pundits coming within striking distance of Ashley Moody. Tuesday’s results show that millions of Floridians can be inspired to come out when candidates embrace true working-class politics, in a way that they simply won’t respond to milquetoast liberals. Even though Florida was home to several hundred thousand more registered Republicans in 2026 as compared to 2022, DSA member Angie Nixon still outperformed centrist liberal Val Demings by a considerable margin. The 2026 midterms are over. Politics doesn’t happen only once every two or four years, though. Our path to victory lies in doing the day-to-day, grassroots work of building the socialist movement in Pinellas County and across the planet, 365 days a year! Read on to learn more about what our chapter was up to over the last month, and what we have coming up next. October Highlights Members of Pinellas DSA, Tampa DSA, and Pasco-Hernando DSA gathered for our Second-Annual Tri-Chapter Social. Our members spoke to thousands of Pinellas residents in October — on doorsteps, on sidewalks, in the streets, and in front of polling locations — in support of multiple initiatives. First, there was the #NoOn3 campaign, which our Electoral Committee initiated in August to get the word out about the cuts coming to municipal governments if Amendment 3 passed. Our Ecosocialist Working Group also circulated a petition as part of the Public Power St. Pete campaign, with the goal of getting a public electrical utility on the ballot for 2028. Local elected official and Pinellas DSA member Richie Floyd hosted a town hall to discuss property taxes, the services funded by them, and the potential impacts of Amendment 3, which yielded a lot of insightful questions and discussion. We also hosted a ballot party for folks to get together, discuss what is on their ballot, and have conversations around less straightforward items like local and state amendments or judges. Stepping outside of the electoral realm, we also hosted the Second-Annual Tri-Chapter Social in Palm Harbor, allowing us to meet up and share food, drinks, and fun with members of Tampa DSA and Pasco-Hernando DSA. And, we tabled at Halloween on Central in St. Pete, where we were able to meet dozens of local progressives that expressed interest in joining our movement! It’s no wonder that Creative Loafing named the DSA ‘Best Inevitability’ this month as part of the 2026 Best of the Bay awards! CAMPAIGN UPDATE: Dump Duke As mentioned above, organizers with our Dump Duke campaign have been hard at work circulating an official petition to get public power on the ballot in St. Pete. Organizers hosted Poll-a-Thons, occupying spots in front of strategically-selected polling locations across the city, hoping to engage voters on the way to cast their ballots. Organizers also circulated the petition at Halloween on Central, helping bring this exciting campaign to even more of our neighbors. Learn more about the petition drive here CAMPAIGN LAUNCH: Apartheid Free Pinellas We’re excited to announce the upcoming launch of a new initiative for our chapter: Apartheid Free Pinellas , which is being managed by our International Solidarity Working Group. Apartheid Free Pinellas is aimed at local businesses in Pinellas County. Campaigners will conduct outreach, helping to raise awareness of common products that have been included on the Boycott, Divestments & Sanctions list, and sharing information about how to replace these products with BDS-compliant alternatives. Participating businesses can display Apartheid Free Pinellas collateral in their stores, letting the community know that it’s safe to shop without concern that you might be inadvertently supporting Israel’s genocide against the Palestinian people. More information will be forthcoming. If you’re interested in getting involved, the first Apartheid Free Pinellas campaign meeting is scheduled for next Wednesday (November 11) at 6:30pm. The meeting will be Zoom only; you can RSVP at the link below. RSVP for the meeting COMMITTEE LAUNCH: Growth & Development PDSA members ready to canvass our neighors. The socialist movement has seen immense growth across the US in 2026. But, if we want to build an organization that can deliver on our ambitious goals, we need to put in place the protocols and procedures that can ensure that we have a healthy, sustainable chapter. To that end, your PDSA comrades are exploring the idea of launching a new committee, focused on growing and developing our chapter into 2027 and beyond. Initiatives that could be overseen by the new Growth & Development Committee may include political education, outreach, text and phonebanking, and planning events aimed at increasing engagement and retaining members. CAMPAIGN UPDATE: Canvassing with the St. Pete Tenants Union PDSA Housing Working Group members conducting outreach to St. Pete tenants.
